External research, clearly attributed

Quantum Health provides educational summaries, not original clinical research. Publication does not prove effectiveness. Read each source in context, check its date and jurisdiction, and distinguish a registered protocol from a completed review.

PubMed study summaries · Search PMC records · Cochrane systematic reviews and protocols · U.S. FDA — regulator guidance · NHS — UK patient information · healthdirect — Australian health information · Cleveland Clinic — external patient education · American Society of Plastic Surgeons · British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons · British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons · StatPearls — NCBI Bookshelf clinical review · MedlinePlus — National Library of Medicine · Wikipedia — enlargement encyclopedia reference · Wikipedia — augmentation encyclopedia reference
PubMed: topic-grouped study findings

This page collects peer-reviewed research on breast enlargement — surgical and non-surgical — indexed in PubMed, the US National Library of Medicine’s database of biomedical literature. In October 2026 we searched PubMed using title and abstract terms covering breast augmentation, breast enlargement, fat transfer and autologous fat grafting, non-surgical enlargement, breast implants and breast fillers. Of 77 unique records retrieved, the most relevant are summarised here, grouped by topic, with a link to each original PubMed record.

What the literature shows in brief: breast augmentation with implants remains one of the most frequently performed aesthetic operations worldwide, with predictable volume but real complication and revision rates. Autologous fat grafting is the best-supported route to lasting volume without an implant, but the gain is modest and complications occur in roughly a quarter of cases in the largest systematic review. External vacuum expansion has produced true tissue growth in small studies, but demands weeks of daily device wear. Injectable fillers are not approved for breast enlargement, and published case series document serious complications. Creams, pills and most devices have no credible supporting trials.

How this page was compiled

Searches were run on PubMed (National Library of Medicine, USA) in October 2026 using title/abstract terms: “breast augmentation”, “breast enlargement”, (“fat transfer” OR “autologous fat grafting” OR “fat grafting”) AND breast augmentation, (“non-surgical” OR filler OR PRP OR “platelet-rich plasma”) AND breast enlargement, and breast implants AND (augmentation OR enlargement). 77 unique records were retrieved; the studies most relevant to breast enlargement are summarised below. Summaries use abstract-level data — consult the full article and current guidelines before drawing clinical conclusions. Inclusion here is not an endorsement of any study or treatment.

Evidence at a glance

The headline findings, by question

Each row links to the PubMed record behind the finding.

The headline findings, by question
QuestionWhat the published evidence showsKey studies
Does fat transfer enlarge breasts?Yes — modestly. The largest systematic review (35 studies, 3,757 women) reported an average 58% fat retention from about 300 mL injected per breast — roughly one cup — with a 27.8% overall complication rate and 92% average patient satisfaction.Seth 2024 (PMID 37166041)
Is fat transfer better than implants?The only randomised trial identified found implants gave more evident and durable augmentation (87.5% vs 70% “excellent” aesthetic outcomes), while fat grafting produced more natural-looking results and better correction of chest-wall deformity.Gentile 2026 (PMID 40908320)
Can a vacuum device enlarge breasts without surgery?A 2000 study reported a stable 55% average size increase after 10 weeks of daily external expansion (10–12 h/day); MRI confirmed growth of fat and fibroglandular tissue. Evidence remains limited and largely developer-led.Khouri 2000 (PMID 10845308); Kardorff 2004 (PMID 16285326)
Do breast fillers work — and are they safe?Hyaluronic acid gel was briefly authorised for breast use in Europe (2008), then withdrawn worldwide after side effects. A 31-patient complication series found 88.9% of conservatively treated aquafilling cases needed reoperation. Regulators advise against fillers for breast enlargement.Siebert 2014 (PMID 24507861); Gierej 2023 (PMID 37721627); Jeyaratnam 2021 (PMID 34849315)
How often do implants need revision?Reported revision rates after primary augmentation are as high as 36%, most commonly for capsular contracture, implant malposition and ptosis of the ageing breast.Denney 2021 (PMID 34121945)
Is “breast implant illness” established?Systemic symptoms attributed to implants are widely reported, but a 2024 Danish review notes the correlation with implants is not established, evidence is limited, and it is not a recognised diagnosis.Borhani-Khomani 2024 (PMID 38808767)
How common is augmentation worldwide?ISAPS 14-year global data show breast augmentation consistently among the top five surgical aesthetic procedures. Implant removal has been the fastest-growing procedure since 2015 (+46.3% over five years).Triana 2024 (PMID 39103642)

Study figures describe the groups studied and may not apply to any individual. Evidence and regulatory positions change — check the linked records and current regulator guidance before acting.

Fat transfer (autologous fat grafting)

Fat transfer removes fat by liposuction from another body area and injects it into the breast. It is the best-documented route to real, lasting volume without an implant — but the gain is modest, and the evidence base, while growing, is still dominated by retrospective series rather than controlled trials.

Fat transfer studies

What fat-grafting research reports

What fat-grafting research reports
StudyDesignWhat it found
Seth I, et al. 2024 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 37166041)Systematic review: 35 studies, 3,757 womenAverage 300 mL injected per breast; 58% volume retention (range 44–83%); 27.8% overall complication rate, fat necrosis the most common (43.7% of complications); radiologic fat necrosis 9.4%, calcification 1.2%; 92% average satisfaction at one year.
Gentile P. 2026 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 40908320)Randomised open-label trial: 95 implants vs 90 lipofilling87.5% of implant patients vs 70% of lipofilling patients had excellent aesthetic outcomes at 12 months. Implant results were significantly more durable; lipofilling results were judged more natural and improved pectus excavatum. Both were safe and effective.
Voglimacci M, et al. 2015 — Aesthetic Surg J (PMID 25908697)Systematic review: 42 articlesEvidence mostly low level (one level-2 study). Two cancers among 2,023 patients (0.09%) with insufficient follow-up for long-term conclusions. Concludes registries with proper follow-up are needed.
Leopardi D, et al. 2014 — ANZ J Surg (PMID 23656507)Systematic review vs implant comparatorsNo comparative studies were found. Fat necrosis, cysts and lumps were the most common complications; reabsorption occurs mainly in the first 12 months; efficacy could not be determined from the available evidence.
Hivernaud V, et al. 2015 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 26085223)Technique reviewHigh resorption remains the central problem of large-volume grafting; refinements in harvesting and graft preparation aim to improve fat viability and long-term success.
Coleman SR, Saboeiro AP. 2015 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 26116935)Technique reviewThe 2009 ASPS Fat Graft Task Force concluded fat grafting may be considered for breast augmentation, with results dependent on technique and surgeon expertise.
Finzi E. 2003 — Dermatol Surg (PMID 12930335)Retrospective record reviewBreast enlargement occurred in 43% of patients after tumescent liposuction of other body areas; 30% gained one cup size or more — an incidental, redistribution-based effect.
Seth I, et al. 2023 — Gland Surg (PMID 36761486)Method paper: hybrid augmentationProposes a preoperative formula to estimate fat-graft volume when combining implants with lipofilling (hybrid breast augmentation).

Non-surgical enlargement: external expansion

External vacuum expansion devices (bra-like systems worn for hours a day) aim to grow tissue through controlled mechanical stretch. Small studies report measurable growth; the regimens are demanding, and critics have questioned measurement consistency.

Expansion studies

External expansion: the published record

External expansion: the published record
StudyDesignWhat it found
Khouri RK, et al. 2000 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 10845308)Single-group study: 17 women (12 completed)A brassiere-like system applying 20 mmHg per breast, 10–12 h/day for 10 weeks: peak increase 98%; after recoil, a stable long-term increase of 55% (range 15–115%). MRI confirmed proportionate growth of adipose and fibroglandular tissue. No adverse events recorded.
Kardorff B, et al. 2004 — JDDG (PMID 16285326)German case report using the same protocolChest circumference at the nipple level remained 4 cm above baseline at three months after oedema resolved. Side effects were limited to transient irritant contact dermatitis and folliculitis.
He Y, et al. 2017 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 28350663)Preclinical/technique studyCombining minimally invasive tissue dissection with external volume expansion generated far more adipose tissue than expansion alone, mediated by release of cell-contact inhibition.
Tebbetts JB. 2001 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 11379562)Critical reviewArgued that claimed non-surgical enlargement largely reflects measurement variability and soft-tissue change rather than reliable true tissue growth — a caution against overstating the early expansion data.
Uyulmaz S, et al. 2020 — Praxis (PMID 33109001)Clinical reviewReviews implant-free cosmetic augmentation: mastopexy for optical lift and lipofilling for volume; large-volume or high-goal augmentation with fat alone remains limited.

Fillers and injectable products

No injectable filler is approved for breast enlargement by major regulators. The published literature documents what happens when fillers are used in the breast: product withdrawal, complication series and reoperation.

Filler safety evidence

What the filler studies report

What the filler studies report
StudyDesignWhat it found
Siebert T, et al. 2014 — Ann Chir Plast Esthet (PMID 24507861)Literature review (Macrolane)Hyaluronic acid gel (Macrolane) received European authorisation for breast augmentation in 2008, then was withdrawn from the worldwide breast-augmentation market after numerous side-effect controversies.
Gierej P, et al. 2023 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 37721627)Observational cohort: 31 women with aquafilling-gel complications88.9% of patients treated conservatively required reoperation, vs 22.7% after radical surgery. Needle aspiration was ineffective and associated with infection (75% positive cultures). More filler injected correlated with more symptoms.
Jeyaratnam S, Joethy J. 2021 — PRS Global Open (PMID 34849315)Case-based reviewDocuments the dangers of filler breast augmentation, consistent with regulator advice against the practice.

Implant augmentation: outcomes, complications and revision

Implant surgery has the largest evidence base of any augmentation method. The studies below cover complication prevention, revision burden, device history, imaging and patient-reported systemic symptoms.

Implant studies

Implant augmentation: the study data

Implant augmentation: the study data
StudyDesignWhat it found
Denney BD, et al. 2021 — Semin Plast Surg (PMID 34121945)ReviewRevision rates after primary augmentation remain as high as 36%; the commonest causes are capsular contracture, implant malposition and ptosis of the ageing breast.
Nava MB, et al. 2017 — Gland Surg (PMID 28497025)Evidence reviewNo high-level evidence identifies a single best technique or implant; complication reduction follows established surgical principles rather than device fashion.
Nahabedian MY. 2019 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 31246764)Review of form-stable implantsReviews diagnosis and management of complications with modern cohesive-gel implants; no implant lasts forever, though devices remain safe and effective per clinical and epidemiologic studies.
Kaoutzanis C, et al. 2019 — Semin Plast Surg (PMID 31632203)Historical reviewTraces implant evolution since 1962, including the silicone-gel controversies, and how successive generations improved safety and aesthetics.
Correia-Sá I, et al. 2013 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 23943050)Case report with histologyPIP implants showed increased rupture and leakage risk; documents clinical, histologic and microbiologic findings after rupture, including siliconoma and lymph-node involvement.
Monstrey S, et al. 2004 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 15108875)Case series: 13 patientsTrilucent (soybean-oil-filled) implants failed because of lipid-oxidation metabolites; UK and Belgian authorities advised removal — a documented device-withdrawal precedent.
Simádo TS. 2021 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 33885442)Clinical algorithmGalactorrhea and galactocele after breast augmentation: a diagnosis and treatment algorithm.
Green LA, et al. 2018 — Clin Imaging (PMID 28918365)Imaging reviewBreast-cancer screening must continue after augmentation; radiologists need familiarity with surgical techniques, implant appearances and MRI findings.
Faguy K. 2018 — Radiol Technol (PMID 29793920)Imaging reviewCatalogues adverse effects and imaging appearances of breast implants for technologists and radiologists.
Borhani-Khomani K, et al. 2024 — Ugeskr Læger (PMID 38808767)Danish reviewSelf-reported systemic symptoms attributed to implants (“breast implant illness”): the correlation is not established, evidence is limited, and the condition is not currently a recognised diagnosis.
Luan J. 2023 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 36396254)Technique reviewEndoscopic-assisted transaxillary augmentation: the axillary approach remains preferred by many patients in Asia; endoscopy improves control and stability of the result.
Bekeny JC, et al. 2020 — Gland Surg (PMID 32775269)Review (transfeminine augmentation)Augmentation for transfeminine patients is technically similar to that for cisgender peers, with equivalent complication rates and documented quality-of-life benefits.
Holst-Albrechtsen S, et al. 2018 — Ugeskr Læger (PMID 29886889)Clinical studyPost-operative infections after cosmetic surgery abroad (“cosmetic tourism”) — treatment abroad carries identifiable infection risk.

Global trends and contemporary benchmarks

Large registry analyses show how often augmentation is performed, how preferences are shifting, and where the field is heading.

Trends

What the registry and benchmark studies report

What the registry and benchmark studies report
StudyDesignWhat it found
Triana L, et al. 2024 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 39103642)ISAPS global statistics, 2010–202334.9 million aesthetic procedures worldwide in 2023. Breast augmentation has remained consistently in the top five surgical procedures for 14 years, with a first decline in the most recent year; implant removal is the fastest-growing procedure since 2015 (+46.3% over five years).
Glicksman CA. 2026 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 41826039)Benchmarks reviewContemporary benchmarks in breast augmentation surgery — current reference points for planning and outcomes.
Lhuaire M, et al. 2019 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 31764702)Technique paperMinimally invasive inframammary breast augmentation — approaches aimed at smaller, hidden incisions.
Lin Y, et al. 2022 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 33403418)Anthropometric studyBody and breast measurements in augmentation planning — objective sizing data supporting implant selection.

Questions

About this research page

PubMed is the US National Library of Medicine’s free index of biomedical literature, covering thousands of peer-reviewed journals. Searching it gives a structured, reproducible view of what has actually been studied — rather than what is advertised.

No. Listing means the study is part of the published evidence base. Individual studies vary in quality — a small case report carries far less weight than a systematic review or randomised trial. Nothing on this page is a recommendation for any individual.

Different designs, patient groups, surgical techniques, measurement methods and eras produce different results. Systematic reviews that pool many studies sit at the top of the evidence ladder; single-centre case series sit lower.

The PubMed search was run in October 2026. New studies are indexed continuously — check PubMed for the latest work, and look for updated systematic reviews and regulator statements.

Each link opens the study’s PubMed record with its abstract. Many full texts sit behind journal subscriptions; ask a librarian, university library or your clinician for access, and treat any claim you cannot verify with caution.

Educational information only — not medical advice

This page summarises published research for general education. It cannot account for your health, anatomy or circumstances, and it does not recommend any treatment. Study figures may not transfer to individuals. Decisions about breast enlargement should be made with a qualified, registered clinician after proper assessment. If you notice a new breast lump or any urgent symptom, seek medical care promptly.

PubMed Central: searchable citation archive

This library indexes every record returned by PubMed Central for the exact phrase “breast enlargement”, retrieved through the NCBI E-utilities on 2026-10-19. It is a reading aid for patients, students and clinicians: each entry links to the original record on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, where the full text can be read in context.

1,874PMC records

How this library was built

The dataset is a complete capture of a single PubMed Central search rather than a hand-picked reading list. The query was the exact phrase "breast enlargement", run against the PMC database with no date limit, subject filter or language filter. Records were retrieved in full, then enriched with citation metadata and abstracts from PubMed where a PMID was available.

The list is broad by design. It includes surgical augmentation, fat transfer, implants, gynaecomastia, neonatal and adolescent breast development, imaging, reconstruction and other uses of the phrase. Inclusion does not mean a study is relevant to you, high quality or current — and it is not an endorsement of any treatment. Abstract text belongs to the original authors and may differ from the published article.

Loading the research library…

Reading research responsibly

PubMed Central is an archive, not a recommendation service. A published paper can be small, observational, outdated or contradicted by later work. Before changing any treatment decision, read the full article, check its date and study design, and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

Cochrane systematic reviews and protocols

This library collects every Cochrane systematic review and registered review protocol that bears on breast enlargement, breast implants and implant-based reconstruction — 3 completed reviews and 4 protocols registered with, or withdrawn by, Cochrane. Each entry links to the full record on cochranelibrary.com, with its DOI and PubMed citation where one exists, so the wording, dates and any later updates can be checked at source.

7Cochrane records
3Completed reviews
4Protocols
20 October 2026Compiled

What this library does and does not mean

Cochrane publishes independent systematic reviews that search for and appraise all available studies on a clinical question. A review here reports what the evidence showed when it was published; a protocol only states what a team intends to review — protocols contain no results, and one entry in this library was withdrawn before any review was written. Nothing here is a recommendation to have or avoid a procedure, and individual suitability always requires assessment by a qualified clinician.

Summaries and key points are condensed from the Cochrane abstracts and record pages for readability. They are not a substitute for the full reviews, which may have been updated since this library was compiled on 20 October 2026. Always read the current version on cochranelibrary.com.

Coverage

What the Cochrane evidence covers

The library is grouped into four areas, from the augmentation question itself to the reconstructive surgery evidence and the protocols still in progress.

Completed reviews

3 completed Cochrane Reviews: wound drains after breast surgery, different implant types, and implants versus autologous tissue flaps after mastectomy.

Augmentation directly

What the reviews say about breast augmentation itself — the drain trials, and why capsular-contracture research (implant insertion funnels) is still only a registered protocol.

Implant type evidence

Five small randomised trials (202 participants) comparing surfaces, fillers and shapes — and the review’s conclusion that implant choice cannot yet be based on randomised evidence.

Reconstruction evidence

Quality of life, satisfaction and complications with implants versus the patient’s own tissue across 35 non-randomised studies and 57,555 participants.

Protocols in progress

Registered protocols on insertion funnels, prepectoral mesh and acellular dermal matrices — what Cochrane is currently examining, with no results yet.

Evidence gaps

Where Cochrane has no review at all: cosmetic augmentation as a procedure, fat transfer for enlargement, breast uplift, fillers and non-surgical options.

All Cochrane records in this library

Grouped by topic. Each entry gives the record type, publication date, a short summary, the main findings or planned methods, and a direct link to the full record, DOI and PubMed citation.

Augmentation and implant technique

Cochrane records that address breast enlargement directly — wound drains after augmentation surgery and the implant insertion techniques used to prevent capsular contracture.

Wound drainage after plastic and reconstructive surgery of the breast

Cochrane Review · Published 21 October 2015

Whether surgical wound drains should be placed after breast augmentation, reduction or reconstruction. Three randomised trials (306 women, 505 breasts) were found out of 190 screened studies — all of them in breast reduction — comparing drains with no drains after surgery.

  • Across the three trials, drains produced no statistically significant improvement in infection, other wound complications, pain, bruising, seroma, haematoma or reoperation.
  • Women who were not drained left hospital a mean 0.77 days sooner (95% CI 0.40 to 1.14 days sooner; low-certainty evidence) — the only significant result.
  • No trials of drains after breast augmentation or breast reconstruction were identified, so the findings apply to breast reduction only.
  • Cochrane concludes that the limited evidence shows no significant benefit of routine post-operative drains, and that augmentation and reconstruction still require investigation.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD007258.pub3 · PMID 26487173

Breast implant insertion funnels for preventing capsular contracture

Cochrane Protocol · Review in progress · Published 30 March 2026

Registered protocol for a review that will assess the effects of breast implant insertion funnels — devices used to guide the implant into place while minimising contact with skin — on capsular contracture rates in women having breast reconstruction or breast augmentation.

  • This is a protocol, not a completed review: no results are available yet.
  • The primary outcome planned is capsular contracture, alongside other complications, with both randomised and non-randomised studies eligible.
  • The protocol anticipates few, if any, randomised trials of funnels, because capsular contracture often appears years after surgery and has many causes.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD016344 · PMID 41909996

Implant types and materials

Cochrane reviews comparing implant surfaces, fillers and shapes, and what the randomised evidence does and does not establish about choosing between them.

Different types of implants for reconstructive breast surgery

Cochrane Review · Published 16 May 2016

Whether different breast implant types — textured or smooth, silicone or saline, anatomical or round, variable or fixed volume — change capsular contracture, complications, satisfaction and quality of life after reconstructive breast surgery. Five randomised trials with 202 participants were found.

  • Every comparison was rated very low quality evidence: the trials were small, at unclear or high risk of bias, and too different from each other to pool.
  • In one trial of 60 women, saline implants had less severe capsular contracture and higher satisfaction than silicone implants, but reinterventions were significantly more frequent with saline.
  • No comparison reached statistical significance for textured versus smooth silicone implants (1 study, 20 women) or anatomical versus round implants (1 study, 36 women).
  • No trials compared fifth-generation silicone implants or different manufacturers; the review concludes that surgeons still cannot counsel women on implant choice on the basis of randomised evidence.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD010895.pub2 · PMID 27182693

Implant-based reconstruction

Reviews and registered protocols on reconstruction after mastectomy: implants versus the patient's own tissue, and the meshes and dermal matrices used to support implants.

Implants versus autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction following mastectomy

Cochrane Review · Published 31 October 2024

Implant-based versus own-tissue (flap) reconstruction after mastectomy — quality of life, satisfaction and short- and long-term complications. Thirty-five non-randomised studies with 57,555 participants met the criteria; no randomised trials were found.

  • Implants may reduce psychosocial well-being (mean difference -4.26 on a 0–100 scale; low-certainty evidence) and sexual well-being (-6.63; low-certainty) versus autologous flaps on BREAST-Q measures.
  • Women may be less satisfied with the reconstruction with implants (-5.96; low-certainty) and with the breast itself (-8.17; very low-certainty).
  • Long-term complications may be more frequent with implants (risk ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.22; very low-certainty), while implant surgery was about 125 minutes shorter (very low-certainty).
  • All evidence came from non-randomised studies (26 at serious overall risk of bias); the review found no superior technique for every woman and called for randomised trials.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD013821.pub2 · PMID 39479986

Mesh for immediate implant-based prepectoral breast reconstruction following mastectomy

Cochrane Protocol · Review in progress · Published 17 June 2025

Registered protocol for a review of biological or synthetic mesh used to support a prepectoral implant (placed above the muscle) in immediate breast reconstruction after mastectomy.

  • This is a protocol, not a completed review: no results have been published.
  • It plans to compare mesh versus no mesh, and biological versus synthetic mesh, for complications, patient-reported outcomes and reoperation after prepectoral reconstruction.
  • Prepectoral placement is one of the placement options also discussed in breast augmentation, so the review will be relevant to implant positioning debate generally.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD015961 · PMID 40525534

Acellular dermal matrices for breast reconstruction surgery

Cochrane Protocol · Review in progress · Published 2015

Registered protocol for a review of acellular dermal matrices (biological meshes derived from human or animal skin) used around implants in immediate prosthetic breast reconstruction after cancer or risk-reducing surgery.

  • This protocol was registered in 2015; no completed review has been published under this title.
  • It plans to compare reconstruction with versus without acellular dermal matrix for seroma, infection, skin flap necrosis, haematoma, reconstruction failure and implant removal.
  • The protocol notes that some studies suggest dermal matrix may raise complication rates, which the review is intended to test.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD011966

Fat transfer

The Cochrane record on fat grafting — withdrawn before any review was completed — and the evidence gap it leaves.

Autologous fat grafting for breast reconstruction

Cochrane Protocol · Withdrawn · Published 29 June 2021

Protocol for a review of autologous fat grafting — transferring the patient's own fat into the breast — for breast reconstruction after cancer surgery. Cochrane withdrew the protocol because the authors were no longer able to complete the review.

  • Cochrane withdrew this protocol: "the authors are no longer able to complete this review", so no Cochrane systematic review of fat grafting exists under this title.
  • The protocol itself was published on 29 June 2021 and remains readable as a record of the intended methods.
  • No Cochrane review has examined fat transfer for cosmetic breast enlargement either.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD010793.pub2

Extracted data

Key findings from the Cochrane records

The statements below summarise what the Cochrane reviews found, and what the protocols and evidence gaps mean for breast enlargement. The right-hand column links to the source record.

Key findings from the Cochrane records
TopicWhat the Cochrane evidence showsSource
Wound drainsRandomised evidence does not support routine drains after breast surgery: in three trials (306 women) drains did not reduce complications, and hospital stay was about 0.8 days shorter without them. Every trial was in breast reduction — none in augmentation.Wound drainage after plastic and reconstructive surgery of the breast
Implant typeNo randomised trial of usable quality establishes one implant type as better than another. All five trials (202 participants) were rated very low quality evidence, and neither textured-versus-smooth nor anatomical-versus-round comparisons reached significance.Different types of implants for reconstructive breast surgery
Implants versus own tissueAcross 35 non-randomised studies (57,555 participants), implants may mean lower psychosocial and sexual well-being and less satisfaction than autologous flaps, but about 125 minutes shorter surgery — with low to very low certainty throughout.Implants versus autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction following mastectomy
Capsular contractureWhether implant insertion funnels reduce capsular contracture is being assessed in a review registered in 2026. No results exist yet, and the protocol expects few randomised trials to be found.Breast implant insertion funnels for preventing capsular contracture
Mesh and dermal matrixTwo registered protocols — mesh for prepectoral support and acellular dermal matrices — still have no completed review, leaving implant-support techniques without a Cochrane synthesis.Mesh for immediate implant-based prepectoral breast reconstruction following mastectomy
Fat transferCochrane has never published a review of fat transfer for breast enlargement. The protocol on fat grafting for reconstruction was withdrawn in 2021 because the authors could not complete it.Autologous fat grafting for breast reconstruction

Findings are paraphrased from Cochrane review abstracts (retrieved via PubMed, October 2026) and are stated with the certainty ratings Cochrane applied to them. Protocols report planned methods only. Verify each point against the linked record on cochranelibrary.com before relying on it.

Where the Cochrane evidence runs out

Cochrane has published no systematic review of cosmetic breast augmentation as a procedure — no review of augmentation techniques, implant placement planes, satisfaction after cosmetic surgery, or long-term outcomes in women who had implants for enlargement rather than reconstruction. The completed reviews here were written for breast reduction and post-mastectomy reconstruction; their findings are evidence about those settings, not direct evidence about augmentation for cosmetic purposes.

There is also no Cochrane review of fat transfer or autologous fat grafting for cosmetic breast enlargement (the reconstruction protocol was withdrawn in 2021), none of silicone gel implants used for cosmetic purposes, none of breast uplift (mastopexy), none of gynaecomastia surgery in men, and none of the non-surgical options discussed elsewhere on this site — fillers, platelet-rich plasma, threads or biostimulators. Absence of a Cochrane review does not mean a treatment works or does not work; it means the question has not been systematically synthesised at this level, and other evidence must be weighed instead.

Search the Cochrane Library yourself

Cochrane’s own search can be run directly: search the Cochrane Library for breast augmentation. Reviews carry identifiers of the form CD012345 (with .pubN suffixes for updated editions); the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) inside the Library also indexes thousands of individual trials on breast implants and breast surgery that no review has yet summarised.

Download and reuse

The structured dataset behind this page is available as JSON. It contains the record list, categories, summaries, key points and extracted findings, with DOI, PMID and source URLs.

Cochrane reviews and protocols are published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in the Cochrane Library and remain the property of Cochrane and the respective authors, with abstracts distributed by PubMed. This library stores only our own summaries, paraphrased key points and links to the publicly available records; full abstracts and review texts are read on cochranelibrary.com.

Breast implants — regulation and approval

How the FDA regulates saline and silicone gel-filled breast implants, which uses are approved, labeling requirements and restrictions on sale.

Breast Implants

Regulatory hub · Content current as of 2023-12-15

The FDA's central breast implant resource. It explains that implants are medical devices placed under breast tissue or chest muscle to increase breast size (augmentation) or to replace tissue removed by cancer or trauma, and links to approvals, labeling, risks, safety communications and post-approval studies.

  • Two implant types are approved for sale in the United States: saline-filled and silicone gel-filled. Both have a silicone outer shell.
  • Implants vary in size, shell thickness, surface texture and shape.
  • The FDA provides this information to support, not replace, the discussion between a patient and a physician.
  • Patients are encouraged to report adverse events through MedWatch.

Read the original on fda.gov →

Types of Breast Implants

Regulatory page · Content current as of 2019-10-23

Describes saline-filled and silicone gel-filled implants, their approved age groups, and the role of breast tissue expanders in reconstruction.

  • Saline-filled implants are approved for breast augmentation in women aged 18 or older and for reconstruction at any age.
  • Silicone gel-filled implants are approved for breast augmentation in women aged 22 or older and for reconstruction at any age.
  • Breast implants are not lifetime devices; the longer they are in place, the more likely removal or replacement becomes.
  • The most frequent complications are capsular contracture, reoperation and implant removal, with or without replacement.
  • MRI remains the most effective method for detecting silent rupture; ultrasound is an acceptable alternative for screening asymptomatic patients.

Breast Implants — Certain Labeling Recommendations to Improve Patient Communication

FDA guidance (2020) · Content current as of 2020-09-29

Final guidance recommending content and format for breast implant labeling, including a boxed warning, patient decision checklist, device description and rupture screening recommendations.

  • Labeling should include a boxed warning and a patient decision checklist.
  • Materials and device descriptions should list the types and quantities of chemicals and heavy metals found in or released by the implant.
  • The guidance underpins the new labeling approved on 27 October 2021.
  • The recommendations supplement the FDA's Saline, Silicone Gel, and Alternative Breast Implants guidance.

Guidance covering the information manufacturers should provide for saline, silicone gel and alternative breast implants, superseding the 2006 version.

  • Applies to saline, silicone gel and alternative breast implants.
  • Supersedes the previous version dated 17 November 2006.
  • Should be read alongside the labeling recommendations guidance.

FDA Strengthens Safety Requirements and Updates Study Results for Breast Implants

Press announcement · Content current as of 2021-10-27

Announcement of orders restricting the sale and distribution of breast implants and approval of new labeling with a boxed warning, patient decision checklist, rupture screening recommendations and a patient device card.

  • Sale and distribution are restricted to providers and facilities that give patients the approved risk information.
  • The patient decision checklist must be reviewed, initialled and signed by the patient and signed by the implanting physician.
  • New labeling includes a device description listing specific materials in the device.
  • The FDA also released updated information on manufacturer post-approval studies.

Breast implants — safety and complications

Known risks, complications, rupture screening, revision surgery, monitoring and long-term follow-up for breast implants.

Risks and Complications of Breast Implants

Regulatory page · Content current as of 2023-12-15

A detailed list of local complications and adverse outcomes reported in at least one percent of breast implant patients, plus sections on reoperation, removal, capsular contracture, rupture, BIA-ALCL, systemic symptoms, breastfeeding and effects on children.

  • Listed complications include asymmetry, breast pain, capsular contracture, deflation, delayed wound healing, extrusion, hematoma, infection, malposition, necrosis, sensation changes, rupture, seroma, wrinkling and unsatisfactory size or style.
  • Capsular contracture is graded I–IV using the Baker scale; grades III and IV are considered severe and may need reoperation.
  • Silicone gel ruptures are often silent; MRI is the most effective detection method and ultrasound is an acceptable alternative for asymptomatic screening.
  • The FDA has not detected an association between silicone gel-filled implants and connective tissue disease, breast cancer or reproductive problems, but notes that larger and longer studies would be needed to rule these out.
  • Some patients report systemic symptoms grouped under the term breast implant illness (BII); causes are poorly understood.
  • Some women can breastfeed after augmentation and some cannot; implant removal without replacement can leave dimpling, concavity, puckering or sagging.

Read the original on fda.gov →

Things to Consider Before Getting Breast Implants

Patient decision guide · Content current as of 2023-03-08

The FDA's pre-surgery checklist covering informed consent, reoperation, monitoring, BIA-ALCL, BII, surgical mesh and the information patients should discuss with their surgeon.

  • Patients should assume additional surgery may be needed because implants are not lifetime devices and complications can occur.
  • Implant removal or replacement may not be covered by insurance, even when a complication occurs.
  • The most common local complications are capsular contracture, reoperation and implant removal; others include rupture or deflation, wrinkling, asymmetry, scarring, pain and infection.
  • BIA-ALCL is a cancer of the immune system, not breast cancer; it is treatable but can be fatal, and treatment usually involves removing the implant and capsule.
  • Surgical mesh used in breast implant surgery has not been approved by the FDA for that use.
  • Silicone implants may require regular MRI or ultrasound screening for silent rupture, which may not be covered by insurance.

Breast Implant Surgery

Regulatory page · Content current as of 2023-08-03

Explains where breast implant surgery can be performed, the FDA position on surgical mesh, and questions patients should ask their surgeon.

  • Breast implant surgery can be performed in a hospital or a surgery centre.
  • The FDA has not cleared or approved any surgical mesh for use with breast implants or in breast reconstruction.
  • Patients are advised to discuss the benefits and risks of mesh with their health care provider.

  • The FDA continually evaluates postmarket safety and manufacturer compliance with approval conditions.

BIA-ALCL and other cancers

Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), squamous cell carcinoma and other lymphomas reported in the capsule around implants.

Questions and Answers about Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL)

Patient and clinician Q&A · Content current as of 2019-10-23

FDA answers on BIA-ALCL: what it is, who is at risk, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and what patients and clinicians should do.

  • BIA-ALCL is a T-cell lymphoma of the immune system, not breast cancer.
  • It is usually found in the fluid or scar tissue near the implant and may spread in some cases.
  • Risk is higher with textured-surface implants than with smooth-surface implants.
  • Main symptoms are persistent swelling, a mass or pain around the implant, often years after surgery.
  • Most patients are treated successfully with surgery to remove the implant and surrounding capsule; some also need chemotherapy or radiation.
  • The FDA does not recommend routine removal of implants in patients without symptoms.

Read the original on fda.gov →

UPDATE: Reports of Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) in the Capsule Around Breast Implants

Safety communication · Content current as of 2023-03-08

Updated safety communication on reports of squamous cell carcinoma and various lymphomas in the scar capsule around breast implants.

  • The communication updates a September 2022 safety communication.
  • The lymphomas described are not the same as BIA-ALCL.
  • The FDA believes cases of SCC and lymphomas in the capsule may be rare.
  • Health care providers should discuss these risks with women who have or are considering breast implants.
  • Patients and providers are asked to report cancers around breast implants to the FDA.

Dermal fillers and injectable silicone

Approved and unapproved uses of dermal fillers, the FDA position on fillers for breast enlargement, and warnings about injectable silicone.

Dermal Fillers (Soft Tissue Fillers)

Regulatory page · Content current as of 2023-07-06

Describes approved facial and hand uses of dermal fillers, the risks, and the FDA's position on unapproved body uses including breast enlargement.

  • Dermal fillers are approved for specific facial uses, lip and cheek augmentation, back-of-hand augmentation, HIV lipoatrophy and contour deficiencies.
  • The FDA recommends against using dermal fillers or any injectable filler to increase breast size (breast augmentation) or for other body contouring.
  • These uses are not approved by the FDA, and the risks of unapproved uses or unapproved products are not known.
  • Injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure and can cause long-term pain, infection, scarring, embolism, stroke and death.
  • Needle-free devices are not approved for injecting dermal fillers, and no dermal filler is approved for over-the-counter use.
  • Removal of filler may require injections, surgery or other interventions, and it may be difficult or impossible to remove permanent fillers.

Regulatory list

The FDA's list of approved dermal fillers and their approved indications, limited to facial tissue and the hands.

  • The list covers approved facial and hand products.

FDA Warns About Illegal Use of Injectable Silicone for Body Contouring and Associated Health Risks

Press announcement and safety communication · Content current as of 2017-11-13

Warning about injectable silicone and products falsely marketed as FDA-approved fillers to enlarge the buttocks, breasts and other body parts.

  • Injectable silicone used for body contouring is not FDA-approved.
  • Serious side effects include ongoing pain, scarring, tissue death, permanent disfigurement, embolism, stroke, infection and death.
  • Complications may occur immediately or weeks, months or years later.
  • Silicone injections for body contouring are often performed by unlicensed providers in non-clinical settings.
  • Injectable silicone differs from the silicone contained inside approved breast implants, because the implant shell keeps the gel from migrating.

Patient-facing advice, decision checklists and how to report adverse events or suspected illegal products.

What to Know About Breast Implants

Consumer update · Content current as of 2025-01-31

Patient-facing overview of implant types, risks, labeling, long-term monitoring, BIA-ALCL and communication with a surgeon.

  • The FDA has approved implants for augmentation, reconstruction after cancer or trauma, correction of developmental defects, and revision of previous surgery.
  • Risks include additional surgery, BIA-ALCL, systemic symptoms (BII), capsular contracture, breast pain, rupture, deflation, silent rupture and infection.
  • Breast implants are not lifetime devices and their lifespan cannot be predicted.
  • Mandatory labeling includes a patient decision checklist, boxed warning and patient device card.
  • Patients with silicone implants are advised to have regular screening for silent rupture and to tell mammography facilities that they have implants.
  • Injectable silicone is not approved for breast augmentation, reconstruction or body contouring.

Regulatory scope and jurisdiction

FDA statements describe the position of the U.S. regulator. Approvals, warnings and labeling requirements can differ in other countries, and the FDA does not regulate where a procedure is performed or by whom outside its jurisdiction. Local registration, advertising rules and clinical standards still apply.

Breast enlargement (implants)

The NHS page on breast enlargement: what the operation involves, costs, implant choices, longevity, recovery, complications, BIA-ALCL, PIP implants, the implant registry and breast screening.

Breast enlargement (implants)

Patient information page · Page last reviewed 2023-09-21

The NHS overview of breast enlargement (also called a boob job or breast augmentation). Implants are inserted to increase size, change shape or make breasts more even. The page covers funding, UK costs, choosing a surgeon and implants, how long implants last, the operation itself, recovery, complications, BIA-ALCL, breast implant illness, PIP implants, the implant registry, breast screening and how to report problems.

  • Breast enlargement is major surgery; results are not guaranteed and there are risks to weigh up.
  • It is usually paid for privately. The NHS may fund it in some circumstances, for example very uneven breasts or no breasts, depending on local rules.
  • In the UK, breast implant surgery costs around £3,500 to £8,000, which does not usually include consultations or follow-up care.
  • Two implant types are offered: silicone (most common in the UK) and saline. Placement is either behind the breast tissue or behind the chest muscle.
  • Implants are not lifetime devices; some women need further surgery after about 10 years.
  • The operation is done under general anaesthetic and takes between 60 and 90 minutes; most people go home the same day or stay overnight.
  • Recovery takes a few weeks: one or two weeks off work, no driving for at least a week, and no heavy lifting or strenuous exercise for at least a month.
  • Reported problems include capsular contracture, rupture, rippling, rotation, nipple sensation changes and reduced breast milk while breastfeeding.
  • BIA-ALCL is an uncommon immune-system cell cancer associated with implants; breast implant illness is a term for symptoms some women report after surgery.
  • PIP implants were banned in the UK in 2010; a ruptured implant should be removed as soon as possible.
  • The Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry (BCIR), set up in 2016, allows implants to be traced if a safety concern arises.
  • Breast screening still matters after implants; mammograms are safe and can be performed differently so as much breast tissue as possible is seen.
  • Check any hospital or clinic in England is registered with the CQC, and that the surgeon is on the GMC specialist register with a licence to practise; always meet the surgeon before the procedure.
  • The MHRA publishes a Cosmetic Breast Augmentation Patient Risk Awareness Tool to help discuss implant risks and keep a record of treatment.

Deciding whether to go ahead

NHS advice on working out whether a cosmetic procedure is right for you, and the steps to take before committing to any procedure.

Is a cosmetic procedure right for me?

Advice page · Page last reviewed 2023-05-09

NHS advice on working out whether a cosmetic procedure is a sound decision: questions to ask yourself, how to research, speaking to an expert, taking time, avoiding pressure and considering mental health.

  • Ask what you want to change and why, how long you have thought about it, what triggered it now, and whether there are other ways to achieve the same change.
  • Ask whether you are expecting the procedure to change your life as well as your appearance, and whether you want it for yourself or to please someone else.
  • Consider all costs, including aftercare, correcting problems and future procedures needed to maintain the look.
  • You should be given a cooling-off period after your consultation to decide.
  • Avoid time-limited offers, extra treatments you had not considered, group treatment events involving alcohol, and mobile services operating in private homes or hotels.
  • Tell the person treating you for a mental health condition, and your cosmetic practitioner, about any mental health problems past or present.
  • Free NHS talking therapies are available for anxiety and depression if appearance concerns are affecting your wellbeing.

Read the original on nhs.uk →

Before you have a cosmetic procedure

Advice page · Page last reviewed 2023-05-22

NHS checklist for people considering a cosmetic procedure, surgical (such as breast implants) or non-surgical (such as dermal fillers or Botox): be clear about why, speak to an expert, research, understand costs, choose a qualified practitioner, ask questions, be cautious with social media and take time.

  • All cosmetic procedures carry some risks, and complications can be serious if they are not done correctly.
  • A GP or mental health professional can be a good first conversation, alongside a consultation with the practitioner.
  • Understand the full costs including aftercare and any future procedures needed to maintain the result.
  • Choose a practitioner who is trained, experienced and has the right insurance to correct anything that goes wrong.
  • Social media influencers are usually paid to advertise services, so research anything found there with extra care.
  • You should be offered a cooling-off period after any consultation, and you can walk away at any point.

Read the original on nhs.uk →

Choosing who will do the procedure

How to check a surgeon or practitioner is properly qualified, registered and insured, and what to ask at a consultation.

Choosing who will do your cosmetic procedure

Advice page · Page last reviewed 2023-06-23

NHS guidance on selecting a practitioner with the right training, skills and insurance: what to ask at a consultation, what the practitioner should explain, checks for cosmetic surgery in England (CQC clinic registration, GMC medical register, RCS certification, BAAPS/BAPRAS membership) and registers for non-surgical practitioners.

  • Always book a consultation with the person who will do the procedure before deciding.
  • Ask how many procedures they have done, their qualifications, common complications, aftercare, what to do if something goes wrong, and the full cost including any further treatment.
  • The practitioner should explain how the procedure is done, how long it takes, whether anaesthetic is needed, expected pain, recovery time, risks, how long results last and what to expect afterwards.
  • Do not pay for a procedure until you have had a consultation.
  • In England, all independent hospitals and clinics providing cosmetic surgery must be registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC), which publishes quality ratings.
  • Only registered doctors can perform cosmetic surgery in England; check the GMC medical register, and note the Royal College of Surgeons certifies cosmetic surgeons against a national standard.
  • For non-surgical procedures, look for practitioners on PSA-accredited voluntary registers such as JCCP or Save Face.
  • Avoid group treatments, treatment vouchers from discount sites, mobile services in homes or hotels, and practitioners who only advertise on social media.
  • Dermal filler complications can be serious, including infection, nerve damage and blindness, so avoid practitioners with only short training courses.

Read the original on nhs.uk →

Cosmetic surgery on the NHS

When the NHS may fund cosmetic procedures such as breast enlargement, and how that differs from reconstructive surgery.

Is cosmetic surgery available on the NHS?

Advice page · Page last reviewed 2023-04-17

Cosmetic surgery is not routinely provided on the NHS, though it may occasionally be funded for psychological or other health reasons. Breast enlargement may be funded for very uneven breasts or no breasts causing significant psychological distress. Reconstructive plastic surgery, such as breast rebuilding after mastectomy or cleft lip and palate repair, is different and often available.

  • Most people who want cosmetic surgery pay for it privately.
  • NHS breast enlargement funding depends on local commissioning rules; your GP can explain the rules in your area.
  • Other examples where the NHS may pay include nose reshaping for breathing problems, ear correction, and breast reduction causing backache.
  • Male breast reduction may be funded for long-standing gynaecomastia that has not responded to other treatments and causes considerable pain or distress.
  • Reconstructive surgery aims to repair or reconstruct missing or damaged tissue after illness, accident or birth defect, and is often available on the NHS.

Read the original on nhs.uk →

Cosmetic surgery abroad

NHS advice on weighing savings against risks when considering cosmetic surgery in another country, including aftercare and flying after surgery.

Cosmetic surgery abroad

Advice page · Page last reviewed 2022-12-14

NHS advice on cosmetic surgery abroad: lower prices must be weighed against risks, follow-up care may be missing or of a different standard, holiday packages need caution, and aftercare, insurance and flying plans should be sorted out in advance.

  • Overseas clinics may not provide follow-up treatment, or not to the same standard as the UK, and may have no UK professional you can see if problems arise.
  • Be cautious of websites selling cosmetic surgery as part of a holiday: meet the surgeon, and do not pay for a hospital you have never seen or a surgeon you have not met.
  • Recovering straight after a holiday is unrealistic; rest is required, with no alcohol, sunbathing, sightseeing or swimming.
  • Find out what happens if there are complications, where follow-ups will be, how easily you could travel back for more surgery, and how much it would cost.
  • Standards and qualifications abroad may differ, so find out how surgeons and clinics are regulated in the chosen country.
  • You should have two consultations with the treating surgeon before surgery, giving a cooling-off period; they should explain the procedure, its limitations, alternatives and risks, and show before-and-after pictures.
  • Travel insurance normally does not cover things going wrong with surgery; check clinic insurance, travel cover and how you would get home in an emergency.
  • Do not fly for 5 to 7 days after procedures such as breast surgery, as air travel plus major surgery increases the risk of a life-threatening blood clot.

What the operation doesImplants are inserted to increase breast size, change their shape or make breasts more even. The procedure is often known as a boob job or breast augmentation.Breast enlargement (implants)
Implant typesThere are two types of implant: silicone and saline. Silicone is the most common in the UK — less likely to wrinkle and feels more natural, but can spread into the breast and cause lumps. Saline is more likely to fold, rupture or deflate over time, but leaked saline is safely absorbed by the body.Breast enlargement (implants)
Implant placementImplants are placed either behind the breast tissue or behind the chest muscle, and size, shape and placement are discussed with the surgeon before the operation.Breast enlargement (implants)
Implant longevityBreast implants do not last a lifetime and will probably need replacing at some point. Some women need further surgery after about 10 years because of implant problems or because the breasts have changed around the implants.Breast enlargement (implants)
The operationBreast implant surgery is usually done under general anaesthetic. An incision is made next to or below the breast, the implant is positioned, and the incision is stitched and dressed. The operation takes between 60 and 90 minutes, with same-day discharge or an overnight stay.Breast enlargement (implants)
RecoveryTake one or two weeks off work, do not drive for at least one week, and avoid heavy lifting or strenuous exercise for at least a month. Stitches come out after one to two weeks, most normal activity resumes after about six weeks, and breasts settle over a few months. Some surgeons recommend a sports bra 24 hours a day for up to three months.Breast enlargement (implants)
Sunbathing and flyingIt is safe to sunbathe and fly if you have breast implants, once recovered. Separately, the NHS advises not flying for 5 to 7 days after breast surgery because of blood clot risk.Breast enlargement (implants)
Common implant problemsBreast implants can cause thick scarring, capsular contracture (the breast feeling hard as scar tissue shrinks around the implant), rupture, creases or folds, rotation, rippling, nipple nerve changes that may be temporary or permanent, and slightly less breast milk while breastfeeding.Breast enlargement (implants)
General surgical risksAs with any operation there is a small risk of bleeding and clots (blood clots can be life threatening), infection treated with antibiotics, and allergic reaction to medicines or products used during surgery such as antibiotics or latex.Breast enlargement (implants)
Rupture detectionA ruptured implant may cause small tender lumps (siliconomas) visible only on breast scans, and the implant will need to be removed. Ultrasound or MRI scans can check whether implants have ruptured.Breast enlargement (implants)
BIA-ALCLThere is an association between breast implants and an uncommon immune system cell cancer called breast implant associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), which develops in the scar tissue around implants in a very small number of people.Breast enlargement (implants)
Breast implant illnessSome women report symptoms after breast implant surgery such as tiredness, anxiety and joint pain, sometimes referred to as breast implant illness.Breast enlargement (implants)
PIP implantsPIP (Poly Implant Prostheses) implants were banned in the UK in 2010 after they were found to contain unapproved silicone gel and to be more likely to split. Anyone with PIP implants should get medical advice, and a ruptured implant should be removed as soon as possible.Breast enlargement (implants)
Implant registryThe Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry (BCIR) was set up in 2016 to record the details of anyone who has breast implants for any reason, so they can be traced if there is a safety concern about a specific implant type.Breast enlargement (implants)
Screening after implantsYou can still get breast cancer after implants and should continue regular breast screening. Mammograms are safe and do not rupture implants; because X-rays cannot pass through implants, the mammogram may be done differently so as much breast tissue as possible can be seen.Breast enlargement (implants)
Reporting problemsProblems with breast implants can be reported through the government's Yellow Card Scheme. Concerns about care can go to the Care Quality Commission, and concerns about a doctor to the General Medical Council.Breast enlargement (implants)
Choosing a clinic in EnglandAll independent clinics and hospitals providing cosmetic surgery in England must be registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC), which publishes quality ratings online.Choosing who will do your cosmetic procedure
Choosing a surgeonCheck the surgeon is registered with the General Medical Council (GMC), listed on the specialist register and holding a licence to practise. Many are also members of BAPRAS or BAAPS, whose registers can be checked, and the Royal College of Surgeons certifies cosmetic surgeons against an agreed national standard.Choosing who will do your cosmetic procedure
Questions for your surgeonThe NHS suggests asking about qualifications and experience, professional association membership, how many breast enlargements they have performed, how many operations involved complications, the implant type, manufacturer and why it is used, the surgical technique and placement, expected results, follow-up if things go wrong, patient satisfaction rates and alternative options.Breast enlargement (implants)
Risk awareness toolThe Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) publishes a Cosmetic Breast Augmentation Patient Risk Awareness Tool (PDF) that patients can use to discuss potential implant risks with their surgeon and keep a record of their treatment.Breast enlargement (implants)
Further informationThe NHS points to patient information from the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons (BAPRAS) and the Royal College of Surgeons for more on breast augmentation and cosmetic surgery.Breast enlargement (implants)
Time to decideYou should be given a cooling-off period after your consultation. The NHS warns against time-limited offers, extra treatments pushed at the clinic, group events involving alcohol, and mobile services operating in private homes or hotels.Is a cosmetic procedure right for me?
PaymentDo not pay for a procedure until you have had a consultation to make sure it is right for you.Choosing who will do your cosmetic procedure
Social media advertisingBe cautious about procedures or clinics found on social media; influencers are usually paid to advertise, and practitioners who only advertise on social media should be avoided.Before you have a cosmetic procedure
Surgery abroadCosmetic surgery abroad can cost less, but follow-up care may be missing or of a different standard, travel insurance normally does not cover surgical complications, and you should have two consultations with the surgeon before surgery. Do not fly for 5 to 7 days after breast surgery.Cosmetic surgery abroad

What this library does and does not mean

healthdirect is a free Australian Government health information service, not a regulator or a clinic. Its pages describe breast augmentation as it is practised and paid for in Australia, what the operation involves and what can go wrong. Nothing here is a recommendation to have a procedure, and healthdirect does not endorse any clinic, surgeon or treatment package.

Summaries and key points are condensed from the healthdirect page for readability. They are not a substitute for the original document, which was last reviewed in November 2025 and may have been updated since this library was compiled on 2026-10-20. Always read the current version on healthdirect.gov.au and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

What breast augmentation is

How healthdirect describes the procedure itself, why people choose it, and the points it says to weigh up before deciding.

What is breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect defines breast augmentation as a form of cosmetic surgery that enlarges the breasts, also called breast enlargement or breast reconstruction. Implants sit either under the breast or under the chest muscle and consist of a silicone shell filled with saline (salty water) or silicone gel. Some surgeons also offer fat grafting, moving fat from another part of the body into the breast. The page notes that reconstruction after mastectomy is a separate topic, and that a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) review led to some breast implants being withdrawn from the Australian market or given conditions on their use.

  • Breast augmentation is cosmetic surgery to make the breasts larger; it is also referred to as breast enlargement.
  • Implants are placed under the breast or beneath the chest muscle and are made of a silicone shell filled with saline or silicone gel.
  • Some cosmetic surgeons offer fat grafting, transferring fat from areas such as the buttocks into the breasts.
  • Reconstruction after a mastectomy uses implants or tissue for a different purpose; that is separate from cosmetic augmentation.
  • After a TGA review, some breast implant products have been removed from the Australian market or had conditions placed on them.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

What are the benefits of breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect states that people consider breast augmentation for many reasons, most commonly a desire to feel more physically attractive or more comfortable with themselves. The page frames the benefit in terms of how the person hopes to feel rather than promising any particular result.

  • Reasons people give include wanting to feel more physically attractive or better about themselves.
  • healthdirect does not guarantee an outcome; expectations should be discussed with a surgeon.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

What should I consider before choosing to have breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect acknowledges social pressure around body shape and asks readers to weigh several points before deciding: implants are not lifelong and usually need replacing after 10 to 15 years; cancer has very rarely arisen in the fluid and scar tissue around an implant; some people are unhappy with how their breasts look afterwards; implants can make breast cancer harder to detect during screening; and breastfeeding may be affected.

  • Implants do not last for life and usually need replacing after 10 to 15 years.
  • There have been rare cases of cancer developing in the fluid and scar tissue around an implant.
  • Some people find the result does not look the way they hoped.
  • Implants can make it harder to detect breast cancer during screening checks.
  • The ability to breastfeed may change after surgery.
  • Body image and social pressure are worth examining before deciding, and counselling is an option.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Current status of breast implant products in Australia

Regulator callout on the healthdirect page · Reviewed November 2025

The healthdirect page carries a callout about a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) review after which some breast implants were removed from the Australian market or had conditions placed on them, and links to the TGA's current status page for the details.

  • The TGA reviewed breast implant products and some were withdrawn from the Australian market or given conditions of use.
  • The TGA website publishes the current status of breast implant products in Australia.
  • The TGA also publishes information on breast implants and anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL).

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

The procedure and preparation

Anaesthetic and implant placement, how to prepare for surgery, choosing a surgeon through AHPRA and RACS, what Medicare covers, and the questions healthdirect suggests asking before surgery.

What does a breast augmentation procedure involve?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

The procedure is normally done under general anaesthetic so the patient sleeps throughout. The surgeon cuts alongside the breast and positions the implant either between the breast tissue and the muscle, or behind the large chest muscle under the breast; the surgeon decides which method suits the patient. Different surgical techniques are available, and the method chosen can affect recovery time.

  • General anaesthetic is usually required, so you are asleep during the operation.
  • The surgeon makes a cut alongside the breast.
  • The implant is placed either between the breast tissue and the muscle, or behind the chest muscle.
  • The surgeon chooses the method, and the technique used can affect how long recovery takes.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

How can I prepare for a breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect advises gathering as much information as possible and preparing by getting physically fit, reaching a healthy weight, trying to stop smoking, asking about medication changes, disclosing health conditions and allergies, and confirming whether you will stay overnight. On choosing a surgeon, it says to pick someone you feel comfortable with who will be honest about benefits and risks, notes that a GP must refer cosmetic surgery patients to their surgeon, and points to the AHPRA register where you can confirm the surgeon is a Fellow of the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) and check for serious disciplinary action. On cost, Medicare generally does not cover cosmetic surgery, private health insurance should be checked, and fees typically include the surgeon, anaesthetist, clinic or hospital, the implants, and medication, dressings and support garments. The page lists questions to ask about implant type, sensation, nipple position and appearance, bruising and pain, plus long-term questions about implant lifespan, breastfeeding, rupture, the likelihood of further operations and the cost of any repeat surgery.

  • Prepare by getting physically fit, maintaining a healthy weight and trying to quit smoking.
  • Ask whether any medications need to change, tell the surgeon about health conditions and allergies, and confirm whether you will stay overnight or go home.
  • Choose a surgeon you feel comfortable with who will discuss benefits and risks honestly.
  • A GP needs to make the referral to the surgeon you choose for cosmetic surgery.
  • Check the AHPRA register to confirm your surgeon is a Fellow of the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) and to see whether serious disciplinary action has been taken.
  • Medicare generally does not cover cosmetic surgery; check your private health policy for any cover.
  • Costs usually include surgeon and anaesthetist fees, clinic or hospital fees, the implants, and medication, dressings and support garments.
  • Ask what implant type is recommended and why, whether sensation will change, how the nipples will be affected, and what bruising, swelling and pain to expect.
  • Ask how long implants last, whether you will be able to breastfeed, how many of the surgeon's patients have had a ruptured or failed implant, how likely further operations are, and whether extra surgery would cost more.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Recovery and warning signs

What to expect after surgery, the support typically needed while healing, and the symptoms that mean you should contact your surgeon or go to hospital.

How soon will I recover?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

Recovery depends on your health before surgery and your surgeon's advice; you may be asked to take a week off work and avoid moderate exercise for around five weeks. Tubes draining fluid, dressings and a compression bandage are common, along with pain and discomfort from swelling and bruising. Pain relief, extra support garments, time off work, help at home and a follow-up visit are often needed. healthdirect says to contact your surgeon or go to a hospital emergency department if you develop fever, severe pain, nausea or vomiting during recovery.

  • Recovery varies with your pre-surgery health and your surgeon's advice.
  • You may be asked to take about a week off work and avoid moderate exercise for around five weeks.
  • Drain tubes, dressings and a compression bandage may be used, and pain, swelling and bruising are normal early on.
  • You may need pain relief, support garments for a few weeks, time off work, help with daily tasks and a follow-up appointment.
  • Fever, severe pain, nausea or vomiting during recovery means you should contact your surgeon or go to a hospital emergency department.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

When should I see my doctor?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect lists the symptoms that mean contacting your surgeon straight away after surgery: a temperature above 38°C or chills; nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath or diarrhoea; heavy bleeding from the wound; bleeding or fluid leakage that starts more than a day after surgery; redness around the implant that is worsening or spreading; and increasing pain or tenderness. In an emergency, go to hospital or call triple zero (000).

  • Contact your surgeon straight away for a temperature over 38°C or chills.
  • Nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath or diarrhoea after surgery need urgent review.
  • Heavy bleeding from the wound, or bleeding or fluid leakage starting more than one day after surgery, needs urgent review.
  • Redness around the implant that worsens or spreads, and increasing pain or tenderness, should be reported.
  • Fever, vomiting or heavy bleeding also warrants going to your nearest hospital.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Complications and risks

The possible problems healthdirect lists after breast implant surgery, from bleeding and infection to rarer serious risks.

What complications can happen?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

Like any operation, breast implant surgery carries risks that should be discussed in detail with a surgeon. healthdirect lists bleeding or a haematoma, infection, changed sensation or numbness in the breast skin or nipple, swelling or a fluid collection, injury to surrounding tissue and implant rupture. Rarer serious risks include an allergic reaction to the anaesthetic, blood clots in the legs that can travel to the lungs, and breast implant-associated cancer — implants previously linked with cancer are no longer available. Severe chest pain or trouble breathing means calling triple zero (000) for an ambulance.

  • Possible problems include bleeding or a haematoma, infection, altered sensation or numbness, swelling or fluid collections, injury to nearby tissue and implant rupture.
  • Rarer serious risks include allergic reaction to the anaesthetic and blood clots in the legs that can travel to the lungs.
  • Breast implant-associated cancer is listed as a rare serious risk; implants linked with cancer in the past are no longer available.
  • Risks should be discussed in detail with your surgeon before you consent.
  • Trouble breathing or severe chest pain requires calling triple zero (000) for an ambulance.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Alternatives and Australian resources

Options other than implants, plus the Australian organisations, fact sheets and helplines healthdirect points readers to.

Are there alternatives to breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect states that breast augmentation may not be right for everyone and lists counselling to help with accepting your body shape, wearing a padded bra, and other types of surgery that do not involve implants as alternatives.

  • Counselling to help you accept your body shape is offered as an alternative.
  • Wearing a padded bra is a non-surgical alternative.
  • Other surgery that does not use implants may also be an option.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Resources and support

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect recommends discussing the decision with your doctor first and links to the Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons, the Agency for Clinical Innovation breast implant safety patient information sheet, an Australian Government fact sheet on cosmetic surgery, and the TGA guide to the five questions to ask before getting a medical implant (available in community languages). It also gives the healthdirect helpline on 1800 022 222 (NURSE-ON-CALL in Victoria), staffed by registered nurses 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

  • Discuss the decision with your doctor before going further.
  • The Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons and the Agency for Clinical Innovation publish patient information on breast implants.
  • The Australian Government has a cosmetic surgery fact sheet, and the TGA publishes a guide to questions to ask before a medical implant.
  • The healthdirect helpline (1800 022 222, NURSE-ON-CALL in Victoria) is staffed by registered nurses 24/7.

What this library does and does not mean

Cleveland Clinic is an academic medical center that publishes patient education; it does not endorse any clinic, surgeon or treatment package, and nothing here is a recommendation to have a procedure. Individual suitability and outcomes require assessment by a qualified clinician.

Summaries and key points are condensed from Cleveland Clinic pages for readability. Coverage

What the Cleveland Clinic information covers

The library is grouped into three areas, from the augmentation procedure itself to implants and fat transfer.

The procedure

What breast augmentation is, the two main types, consultation, preparation, anaesthesia, incisions, implant placement and aftercare.

Recovery and risks

Time off work, recovery timelines of six to eight weeks, side effects, complications from capsular contracture to rupture, and when to call the doctor.

Safety concerns

BIA-ALCL and textured implants, cancer screening and mammograms with implants, breastfeeding effects and long-term implant monitoring.

Breast implants

Implant types, age limits for saline and silicone, natural look and feel, sizing, placement, incision options and how long implants last.

Fat transfer

Candidacy, the liposuction and injection technique, lifelong results, one-to-two-cup-size limits, risks and mammograms afterwards.

Decisions and costs

Questions to ask at consultation, why people choose augmentation, insurance coverage, reversibility and breastfeeding considerations.
