Breast augmentation

The Cleveland Clinic overview of breast augmentation: what it is, the two main types (implants and fat transfer), why people choose it, consultation, preparation, the operation itself and aftercare.

Breast Augmentation: What it is, Types, Surgery & Recovery

Treatment overview · Medically reviewed, last updated 2021-08-24

Cleveland Clinic's overview of breast augmentation, a common cosmetic surgery that uses breast implants or fat transfer to increase the size and shape of the breasts. It covers the implant types (saline, structured saline, silicone, form-stable, round, smooth, textured), fat transfer augmentation, why people choose the procedure, how common it is, the consultation and preparation, the steps of surgery (anaesthesia, incision, implant placement, closing), what happens afterwards, benefits, side effects and complications, cancer screening with implants, recovery time, when to call the doctor, insurance, reversibility and breastfeeding.

  • Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure that increases the size and shape of your breasts using breast implants or fat transfer.
  • Two main types: breast implants and fat transfer augmentation; certain implants are only FDA-approved for certain ages.
  • Saline implants are filled with sterile salt water; if they break, your body absorbs the saline naturally.
  • Silicone implants are filled with silicone gel; if they break the gel can stay in the shell or leak into the breast, and regular checks with your surgeon may be needed.
  • Form-stable ("gummy bear") implants keep their shape even if the shell breaks, are made of thicker gel and need a longer incision.
  • Round implants make breasts look fuller and don't change the look of the breast if they rotate; smooth implants feel softest and move most naturally.
  • Textured implants encourage scar tissue to adhere so they move less, but breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) occurs most frequently with textured surfaces.
  • In fat transfer augmentation, liposuction takes fat from the belly, flanks, back or thighs and injects it into the breasts; it is usually for a relatively small increase in size.
  • People choose augmentation to change size, correct asymmetry, restore size after pregnancy or weight loss, correct unevenness after other breast surgery, or to improve confidence.
  • Around 300,000 people in the United States have breast augmentation surgery every year; it is the most popular type of cosmetic surgery.
  • At consultation your surgeon reviews medications, allergies, smoking, prior surgeries and breast history; you should have realistic expectations and be in good mental and physical health.
  • Preparation may include a blood test, adjusting medications, stopping smoking, avoiding aspirin and anti-inflammatory drugs, and stopping recreational drugs.
  • Arrange a driver and someone to stay the first night; take at least three days off work, or at least three weeks for a labour-intensive job.
  • Surgery is done under general anaesthesia or IV sedation; incisions can be at the inframammary fold, around the areola (periareolar) or through the armpit (transaxillary).
  • Implants are placed either under the breast tissue in front of the muscle or behind the pectoral muscle, depending on implant type and how much size is increased.
  • Stitches are usually removed in about one week; no heavy lifting for at least four weeks and no sports for up to six weeks.
  • Full recovery takes about six to eight weeks on average; recovery varies by augmentation type and overall health.
  • Side effects include soreness, nipple sensitivity, bruising, bleeding and swelling; immediate complications include infection, wound healing issues and hematoma.
  • Longer-term complications include capsular contracture (scar tissue), implant sagging, symmastia, seroma (fluid around the implant) and implant rupture or deflation.
  • BIA-ALCL is a rare immune-system cancer reported with textured implants; symptoms such as size or shape changes, swelling or lumps may appear two to eight years after surgery.
  • Breast implants are not guaranteed to last a lifetime; pregnancy, weight loss and menopause may change the appearance of augmented breasts.
  • Implants can make mammograms harder to read; the American College of Radiology and related bodies recommend breast examinations at an ACR-accredited facility, which can take special views.
  • Breast augmentation is usually considered elective cosmetic surgery, so insurance generally does not cover it; reconstruction after cancer may be covered.
  • Yes, augmentation is reversible: implants can be removed, replaced or repositioned by a plastic surgeon.
  • Augmentation can affect nerves and ducts involved in lactation; implants placed below the muscle affect milk production less than those above, and periareolar incisions are more likely to reduce milk production.

Breast implants

Cleveland Clinic information on breast implants themselves: who gets them, implant types, natural look and feel, sizing and placement, how long they last, advantages, risks and recovery.

Breast Implants: Types, Surgery, Recovery & Risks

Treatment overview · Medically reviewed, last updated 2021-08-31

Cleveland Clinic's guide to breast implants: artificial silicone shells filled with silicone gel or saline, inserted by plastic surgeons for augmentation or reconstruction. It covers candidacy, reasons for getting implants, how common they are, how long implants last, which implants feel and look most natural, age limits for saline and silicone implants, sizing and placement, the four incision types, the procedure, recovery timeline, follow-up schedule, advantages, risks and the questions to ask your provider.

  • Breast implants are artificial devices (prostheses): silicone shells filled with silicone gel or saline, inserted by plastic surgeons.
  • Candidates should be finished developing, in good physical health and have realistic expectations.
  • People get implants to restore previous breast size after pregnancy, weight loss or aging, to correct asymmetry, to restore breasts after mastectomy, or to boost confidence.
  • About 3.5 million people in the United States have breast implants; roughly 60% contain silicone gel; about 35 million people worldwide have implants.
  • Breast augmentation is the procedure that makes breasts larger; breast implants are the devices used in many augmentations.
  • Implants typically last about 10 years; the older they get, the more likely they are to rupture; signs include changes in size, shape, firmness or swelling, though rupture can also have no signs.
  • Silicone implants tend to feel more natural than saline; smooth shells feel more natural and move more freely than thicker textured shells.
  • The FDA approved highly cohesive silicone gel ("gummy bear") implants in 2012; teardrop-shaped implants usually come with a textured shell so they don't rotate.
  • You must be at least 18 years old for saline-filled implants and the FDA recommends at least 22 years old for silicone-filled implants.
  • Providers assess mental health and social factors, including body dysmorphic disorder concerns and whether a partner is pressuring the decision.
  • Implant size is matched to body structure: larger implants suit broader shoulders or wider hips, while oversized implants on a small frame can cause back, neck and shoulder pain.
  • Preoperative sizing lets you try sample implants under clothing in front of a mirror before choosing size and shell type.
  • Two placement options: submuscular (beneath chest muscles) and subglandular (between chest muscles and breast tissue).
  • Four incision types: periareolar (around the areola), inframammary (breast crease), transaxillary (armpit) and transumbilical (belly button).
  • After surgery breasts are wrapped in a supportive bra or compression band; you need a driver and someone to care for you for the first 24 hours.
  • Full recovery is on average six to eight weeks; the first several days are the most painful, with swelling, bruising and slight incision bleeding.
  • Pain usually decreases after five to seven days; light daily activities and desk work can resume after one to two weeks, but avoid running, heavy lifting and arms above head.
  • Return to work is typically between two and six weeks, depending on how physically demanding the job is.
  • Advantages: implants are durable (about 10 years), implant surgery has a relatively low risk of complications, and implants can boost self-esteem.
  • Risks include short- and long-term complications, the need for additional surgery (removal, replacement, scar-tissue removal or repositioning), BIA-ALCL and breastfeeding complications.
  • Implants increase size but do not lift; a breast lift can be combined if sagging is a concern.
  • Follow-up: bandages and possibly stitches removed after one to two weeks, then reviews at four to six weeks, three months and six months.
  • Ask which implant type and size suit your body, how long implants last, what happens on rupture, what autologous breast augmentation is, and the full list of risks.

Fat transfer breast augmentation

Cleveland Clinic information on using your own fat (liposuctioned and reinjected) to enlarge the breasts: candidacy, the procedure, how long results last, benefits, downsides, recovery and mammograms afterwards.

Fat Transfer Breast Augmentation: Procedure, Results & Risks

Treatment overview · Medically reviewed, last updated 2022-08-18

Cleveland Clinic's guide to fat transfer breast augmentation: liposuction removes fat from areas such as the belly, hips, back, legs or arms, and the purified fat is injected into the breasts to increase cup size by one to two sizes. It explains how the procedure differs from implants and reconstruction, who is and is not a candidate, how the outpatient surgery is performed, that results are lifelong (settling over up to six months), the risks, benefits and cons, recovery, when to call the doctor, and the effect on breast cancer risk and mammograms.

  • A fat transfer breast augmentation uses fat from your own body to enlarge your breasts: fat is suctioned from several areas and injected into the breasts.
  • Breast augmentation is cosmetic surgery to increase breast size and enhance shape; the two types are breast implants and fat transfer.
  • Breast augmentation is for healthy people improving appearance and is not medically necessary; breast reconstruction after cancer always uses implants.
  • Good candidates want slightly larger breasts without implants; people with little body fat, obesity, drastic weight fluctuations or who smoke may not be suitable.
  • It is an outpatient procedure under general anaesthesia: fat is harvested by liposuction, purified in a centrifuge, then injected into different tissue layers of the breasts.
  • Results are described as lifelong: fat cells settle over up to six months and remain for life, though extra fat is injected because some cells die after transfer.
  • Risks include bleeding and bruising, fat cell death (necrosis) or fat migration, infection, and benign breast cysts or calcifications.
  • Benefits over implants: a natural look and feel, the donor areas (belly, hips, back, legs or arms) become slimmer, and no implant-related risks such as rupture or capsular contracture.
  • Cons: only one or two cup sizes of increase, breasts may still sag (a breast lift would be needed), and multiple procedures may be required.
  • Recovery: chest wrapped with an elastic bandage and surgical bra, about a week off work, pain bruising and swelling for up to three weeks, swelling may last up to six months.
  • Sleep on your back, take antibiotics and pain relievers as directed, and wear loose clothing to ease recovery.
  • Call your provider for excessive bleeding, swelling or bruising, nausea and vomiting, severe pain, or signs of infection such as yellow discharge or fever.
  • Fat transfer does not increase breast cancer risk and mammograms still work well afterwards, though it can cause microcalcifications that may need further tests such as ultrasound, MRI or needle biopsy.

What this library does and does not mean

ASPS is a professional membership organization for board-certified plastic surgeons, not a government regulator and not a clinic. Its pages describe breast augmentation as performed by its member surgeons and the standards it expects of them. Nothing here is a recommendation to have a procedure, and ASPS does not endorse any individual surgeon, clinic or product.

Summaries and key points are condensed from ASPS pages for readability. They are not a substitute for the original documents, which may have been updated since this library was compiled on 2026-10-20. Always read the current version on plasticsurgery.org and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

Breast augmentation

The ASPS overview of breast augmentation: what the operation is, what it can and cannot do, who makes a suitable candidate, what happens at consultation and the questions patients are advised to ask.

Breast Augmentation (Augmentation Mammaplasty)

Procedure overview

The ASPS overview of breast augmentation: a procedure that uses breast implants or fat transfer to increase breast size. It explains that augmentation can restore volume lost after weight reduction or pregnancy, create a rounder shape or correct natural asymmetry, lists what the surgery can and cannot achieve, and points patients to implant safety, fat transfer and breast lift information.

  • Breast augmentation (also called augmentation mammaplasty) uses breast implants or fat transfer to increase the size of the breasts.
  • It can restore volume lost after weight reduction or pregnancy, achieve a rounder shape, or improve natural size asymmetry.
  • When fat from another part of the body is used, the procedure is called fat transfer breast augmentation.
  • Surgery can increase fullness and projection, improve the balance of breast and hip contours, and enhance self-image and confidence.
  • Augmentation does not correct severely drooping breasts; a breast lift may be required alongside it for sagging breasts to look fuller and lifted.
  • A lift can often be done at the same time as augmentation, or may require a separate operation.
  • Implants are also used for breast reconstruction after mastectomy or injury.

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Breast Augmentation Candidates

Patient guidance

ASPS guidance on who may be a candidate for breast augmentation. The page stresses that the procedure is deeply personal and should be chosen for oneself, lists the medical and developmental factors surgeons look for, and describes the common reasons people seek augmentation.

  • The decision is deeply personal and should be made for yourself rather than to satisfy someone else.
  • Candidates should be physically healthy and not pregnant or breastfeeding.
  • Breasts should be fully developed and expectations should be realistic.
  • Common motivations include dissatisfaction with small size, loss of shape or volume after pregnancy or weight loss, and changes with aging.
  • Other reasons include an empty upper breast, asymmetry, or one or both breasts failing to develop normally.
  • Reviewing before-and-after photos and recovery information beforehand helps set reasonable expectations.

Breast Augmentation Consultation

Patient guidance

What to expect at a breast augmentation consultation: the topics patients should be ready to discuss, the medical history the surgeon collects, and the physical assessment and measurements used to make a recommendation.

  • Be ready to discuss your motivation, expectations and the outcome you want.
  • Disclose medical conditions, allergies, previous treatments, medications, supplements and any substance use.
  • Share family history of breast cancer and the results of previous mammograms or biopsies.
  • The surgeon evaluates general health and risk factors, then takes detailed breast measurements and photographs.
  • The examination covers size, shape, skin quality and nipple-areola placement before treatment is recommended.
  • The surgeon discusses the expected outcome, risks and complications, and offers a written question checklist.

Questions to Ask Your Plastic Surgeon

Question checklist

The ASPS checklist of questions patients should take to a breast augmentation consultation, covering surgeon credentials, facility accreditation, the surgical plan, recovery support, risk handling and long-term considerations.

  • Verify board certification by the American Board of Plastic Surgery and plastic-surgery-specific training.
  • Ask about years of surgical training and where the surgeon has hospital privileges.
  • Confirm the surgical facility is accredited, state-licensed or Medicare-certified.
  • Discuss candidacy, the recommended implant shape, size and texture, and incision and placement choices.
  • Ask how long recovery takes, what help you will need, the risks, and how complications would be handled.
  • Ask about possible future operations, effects on breastfeeding, and how results change over time and after pregnancy.

Breast implants

ASPS information on the implants themselves: fill types (saline, silicone, structured), shapes and surfaces (form-stable, round, smooth, textured), FDA age approvals and surface-related safety concerns.

Types of Breast Implants

Device overview

ASPS guidance on the main implant options: fill type (saline, silicone gel, structured saline) and shape or surface (form-stable "gummy bear", round, smooth, textured), with the FDA age approvals and the main trade-offs of each choice.

  • Saline implants are filled with sterile salt water; if they leak the implant collapses and the body safely absorbs the fluid.
  • Silicone gel implants are designed to mimic the feel of natural tissue; a leak may stay contained and the implant does not collapse.
  • Structured saline implants contain an inner matrix intended to give a more natural feel.
  • Form-stable "gummy bear" implants keep their shape even if the shell breaks; they use a firmer gel, need a longer incision and shaped versions can rotate.
  • Round implants look fuller and do not rotate out of place; smooth implants feel softest but may ripple, while textured implants grip tissue.
  • Textured surfaces are the surface most associated with breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL).

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Risks and safety

ASPS information on the risks of augmentation and implant-specific safety concerns, including capsular contracture, rupture, BIA-ALCL, BIA-SCC, breast implant illness and FDA screening intervals.

Breast Augmentation Risks and Safety

Safety guidance

The full list of risks ASPS publishes for breast augmentation — from anesthesia complications and capsular contracture to implant-associated cancers and breast implant illness — together with the reminder that implants are not lifetime devices and that FDA-recommended screening applies to silicone implants.

  • Common risks include anesthesia complications, bleeding or hematoma, infection, capsular contracture, implant rupture, changes in sensation, poor scarring and possible revision surgery.
  • Rare cancers of the implant capsule (BIA-ALCL and BIA-SCC) and systemic symptoms described as breast implant illness are acknowledged.
  • Most people with implants never experience serious complications, but FDA-approved devices still carry documented risks.
  • Implants are not guaranteed for life; future replacement surgery may be needed.
  • Ongoing breast-health exams and implant-condition checks are needed, and pregnancy, weight loss and menopause change appearance over time.
  • Routine screening matters because some ruptures produce no symptoms.

Preparation, procedure and recovery

Practical steps around the operation itself: pre-operative preparation, the five surgical steps (anaesthesia, incision, placement, closure, result), immediate aftercare and the recovery timeline.

Breast Augmentation Preparation

Pre-operative guidance

The medical and lifestyle steps ASPS advises before breast augmentation: tests and medication changes, stopping substances that increase bleeding, choosing an accredited surgical facility and arranging post-operative support.

  • You may need blood tests and adjustments to your medications, including stopping certain drugs.
  • Stop smoking and avoid aspirin and anti-inflammatory drugs that can increase bleeding.
  • Recreational drugs such as cocaine must be stopped before surgery.
  • Breast augmentation should be performed in an accredited outpatient or ambulatory surgical center or a hospital.
  • If going home the same day, arrange a driver and someone to stay with you for at least the first night.

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Breast Augmentation Procedure Steps

Procedure steps

The five steps of breast augmentation as set out by ASPS — anaesthesia, incision, implant placement, closing the incisions and the immediate result — with the incision and placement options and a caution about the transumbilical approach.

  • Step 1: anesthesia with IV sedation or general anesthesia, selected for the patient.
  • Step 2: incisions placed in discreet locations — around the areola (peri-areolar), in the breast fold (inframammary) or in the armpit (axillary).
  • Step 3: the implant is placed either under the pectoral muscle (submuscular) or behind the breast tissue over the muscle (submammary).
  • Step 4: incisions are closed with layered sutures plus skin sutures, adhesive or tape; scar quality depends on genetics, nicotine use and infection.
  • Step 5: results are visible immediately after surgery.
  • The belly-button (transumbilical) incision approach is associated with a higher complication rate.

Breast Augmentation Recovery

Recovery guidance

What to expect straight after breast augmentation: dressings and support garments, monitoring and discharge timing, the instructions and medications you go home with, and the pain and activity timeline during healing.

  • Breasts are wrapped in gauze with an elastic bandage or support bra to limit swelling.
  • Patients are monitored in recovery and typically discharged about an hour after surgery once stable.
  • You receive written post-operative instructions, a follow-up appointment and possibly pain medication and an antibiotic.
  • The support garment or bandeau should be worn around the clock as directed; incision-care instructions vary by surgeon.
  • Take it easy for the first several days because of bleeding risk around the implant pockets, and resume exercise only when cleared.
  • Acute pain usually subsides after one to five days, while soreness and swelling may persist for a few weeks.

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Breast Augmentation Results

Results guidance

How breast augmentation results settle over time: shape finalising over the first weeks as swelling resolves, incision marks fading slowly, the follow-up cadence, and the fact that implants are not lifetime devices and results change with aging.

  • Breasts are larger right away, but the final shape takes a few weeks as swelling subsides and the skin stretches.
  • Some patients, such as those with asymmetry or very small starting breasts, may need a bandeau to help shape the result.
  • Incision lines can take months — even a couple of years — to fade.
  • Optimal results depend on following post-operative instructions and attending follow-up visits.
  • Implants are not lifetime devices; annual exams evaluate breast health and implant integrity.
  • Aging, weight fluctuation, hormones and gravity change the result; some patients later choose a lift or implant exchange.

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Fat transfer breast augmentation

ASPS information on enlarging the breasts with your own fat: liposuction harvesting, reinjection, who it suits and the research it references.

Fat Transfer Breast Augmentation

Procedure overview

The ASPS page on fat transfer breast augmentation: liposuction is used to harvest fat from elsewhere in the body and reinject it into the breasts, offered as an option for people wanting a relatively small, natural-looking increase in size.

  • Fat is taken by liposuction from other parts of the body and injected into the breasts to enhance them.
  • It is an option for people looking for a relatively small increase in breast size.
  • It is described as a choice for those who would prefer natural results.
  • ASPS cites research on pre-expansion for mega-volume transfer, fat transfer as an alternative to implants, and techniques that substantially increase breast size using the patient's own fat.
  • When fat transfer is used, the procedure is referred to as fat transfer breast augmentation rather than augmentation mammaplasty with implants.

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Cost and choosing a surgeon

What ASPS publishes on augmentation fees, what is and is not included, insurance coverage, and the credentials an ASPS member plastic surgeon must hold.

Breast Augmentation Cost

Cost guidance

ASPS guidance on the cost of breast augmentation, including its published average surgeon fees for implant and fat-grafting augmentation, the expenses those figures exclude, and the insurance position for cosmetic surgery.

  • Published average costs reflect surgeon fees only, not the total price of the procedure.
  • Anesthesia, operating-room or facility fees, medical tests, garments, prescriptions and related expenses are excluded.
  • The surgeon fee varies with experience, procedure type and geographic location.
  • Many surgeons offer patient financing plans.
  • Most insurance plans do not cover cosmetic augmentation, related complications or revision surgery.
  • Some carriers exclude breast-disease coverage for implant patients.

Read the original on plasticsurgery.org →

Choosing a Plastic Surgeon

Credential guidance

The credentials ASPS says patients should look for: an ASPS member plastic surgeon board-certified by the American Board of Plastic Surgery (or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada), with the required training, exams, continuing education and accredited facility standards.

  • Choose an ASPS member plastic surgeon board-certified by the American Board of Plastic Surgery or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada.
  • Certification requires at least six years of surgical training after medical school, including a minimum of three years of plastic surgery residency.
  • Surgeons must pass comprehensive oral and written exams and graduate from an accredited medical school.
  • Continuing medical education including patient safety must be completed every year.
  • Surgery must be performed in accredited, state-licensed or Medicare-certified facilities.
  • The ABPS is recognized by the ABMS, and no ABMS-recognized certifying board has "cosmetic surgery" in its name.

British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons

This page works through the patient guide published by the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons (BAPRAS) — the four-part guide to breast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation, or BBA): what the operation is, how to choose a surgeon, implant techniques, the complications that can occur and the long-term consequences. Every part is summarised here and linked to the original, so the current wording can always be checked at source.

BAPRAS describes breast enlargement as a potentially life-enhancing procedure — but also as a big decision: major surgery with potential risks, and a result that cannot be guaranteed. The guide was edited by Lee Martin and Emma de Sousa, with contributions from Julie Doughty, Paul Harris, Mark Henley, Nigel Mercer, Charles Nduka, Mary O’Brien, Caroline Payne and Ruth Waters, and was last updated in 2021. A printed copy of the guide is available from the BAPRAS secretariat, and a PDF is published alongside the online version.

This summary is educational. It does not replace the discussion you should have with your own surgeon, and it does not constitute medical advice or a recommendation of any procedure, surgeon or clinic.

The four-part guide

What the BAPRAS guide covers

From the first consultation to the decisions that stay with you for decades.

The decision

Who the guide is for, what breast augmentation can and cannot achieve, and why realistic expectations matter.

Consultation & cooling-off

How to seek a consultation, what happens at it, and why a cooling-off period of at least two weeks is required.

Implant techniques

Incisions, placement behind the breast or muscle, dual plane, and how implant type, size, shape and texture are chosen.

The operation

Anaesthetic, time in hospital, recovery week by week, and how scars typically evolve over the first year.

Complications

Reported frequencies for bleeding, infection, capsular contracture, sensation change and rupture — plus BIA-ALCL and breast implant illness.

Long-term questions

Mammography with implants, alternatives such as lipofilling and uplift surgery, and the national implant registry.

What this page is — and is not

This is a condensed, section-by-section summary of BAPRAS patient information written for people considering breast enlargement in the United Kingdom. Figures such as complication frequencies are those published in the guide; UK practice, funding rules and professional registers differ between countries, so local standards still apply wherever a procedure is performed.

Nothing here is a personal assessment of suitability. That can only be done in a consultation with a qualified, registered surgeon who examines you.

What breast augmentation is

Breast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation or BBA) is an operation to enlarge the breasts, usually by inserting an implant beneath the breast to make it look larger. It can enlarge breasts that have always been small, and it can also fill out breasts that used to be larger — for example breasts that have emptied out after pregnancy. The procedure reshapes breasts to some extent and can be used to correct breasts that are of unequal size.

An alternative to enlargement with an implant is fat transfer, sometimes called lipomodelling, lipofilling or fat grafting: fat taken from elsewhere on the body is injected into the breast area. Fat transfer may be appropriate for a few people but is not suitable for all, often requires more than one episode of surgery, and can also be combined with an implant augmentation.

Patients who have breast augmentation tend to be pleased with the results, but the guide is explicit that expectations must be realistic. You need to understand what can and cannot be achieved, the limitations of surgery, and the long-term consequences of having breast implants.

Next steps

Getting to a decision

The BAPRAS guide sets out a deliberate, unhurried path from first enquiry to the operating table.

01

Find a surgeon

Your GP may be able to suggest surgeons locally, or you can approach a private hospital or clinic directly. If you do, make sure your initial consultation is with the surgeon who will actually do the operation. Your surgeon will normally seek permission to write to your GP afterwards.

02

Attend a full consultation

You will be asked what is bothering you about your breasts and what you expect from surgery, must share your full medical history, and will be examined with measurements taken. Discussion follows about implant shapes, possible sizes and the position of the pockets behind your existing breast tissue. A consultation fee is normal.

03

See the likely result

Some surgeons use implant sizers in a bra, others 3D photography. This is only a guide — the same implant can look very different in different people. You should be told about the operation, the expected outcome and the possible risks and complications.

04

Take the cooling-off period

You should be given a cooling-off period of at least two weeks before surgery and offered a second consultation. You should not feel rushed into surgery — if you are, walk away.

Why there is a cooling-off period

Breast augmentation is a lifetime commitment and must not be considered a one-stop permanent solution. You need to be making the appropriate choice and understand all the implications of the surgery you are considering — including that you will need revision surgery as the years go by, and that you must be prepared personally and financially for this.

Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation. If you are not offered a cooling-off period, or you are put under pressure to proceed, the guide’s advice is simple: walk away.

Checks, costs and funding

Before you commit

Before you commit
TopicWhat the BAPRAS guide says
Checking your surgeonAll surgeons should be listed with the General Medical Council (GMC). Check the register at gmc-uk.org using “Check a doctor’s registration status”. Under “Status” they should be listed as “Registered with a license to practise; this doctor is on the specialist register”. Surgeons may also be registered with the Association of Breast Surgery (ABS), BAAPS and/or BAPRAS — members of these organisations hold a standard set of recognised qualifications. It is perfectly reasonable to ask about a surgeon’s experience and qualifications.
Internet searchesInformation found through search engines may be promotional in nature; some surgeons and services pay for their listing. A prominent listing is a measure of marketing ability, not of service quality.
CostAn approximate cost should be obtainable from your local private hospital or the surgeon’s secretary before your consultation, and you should expect to pay a fee for the consultation itself. After your consultation(s), if you plan to go ahead, you should be given a written quote for the planned care.
Deposits and inducementsAvoid any deal asking for a non-refundable deposit, and do not accept a financial inducement or time-limited deal — even offering to refund the consultation fee if you proceed with surgery is considered an inducement and is against GMC guidance.
Package pricesIt is appropriate to be offered a package covering the whole process and the cost of treating any complications arising in the initial weeks after surgery. You should be told exactly what the package includes. The cheapest deal may not be the best: cosmetic surgery is a significant financial commitment, and you will need to pay for further surgery in the future.
NHS fundingCosmetic breast augmentation is not available on the NHS, so you will normally consult and pay privately. Exceptional circumstances can include very uneven breasts (a significant difference in size), having no breasts, or treatment as part of a breast reconstruction care plan — your GP can explain the rules in your area.
Surgery abroadIf you go abroad for breast augmentation, be aware that on return to the UK only emergency complications will be dealt with by the NHS.

Summarised from the BAPRAS patient guide. Cosmetic-surgery funding, regulation and professional registers differ between countries — verify the current position in your own jurisdiction.

Implant techniques

Breast enlargement involves placing an implant under the breast tissue to increase the size and shape of the breast. Implants are usually inserted through an incision under the breast at the crease, but they can also be placed through an incision in the armpit or around the nipple.

Behind the breast (sub-glandular)

Placing the implant behind the breast, on top of the chest wall muscle, is considered the simplest of the available enlargement procedures and is less likely to cause significant discomfort. This route is also effective for patients with some drooping of the breasts.

Behind the muscle (sub-muscular)

Placing the implant behind the breast muscle gives more padding or coverage for the implant. This can help slender patients and those with very little breast tissue, because it reduces the chances of being able to feel or see the implant under the breast tissue.

Dual plane augmentation

Surgeons often combine the two routes, placing the implant partly behind the breast and partly behind the muscle, to try to give the benefits of both — this is called a dual plane augmentation. If implants are inserted behind the muscle they are likely to move when the muscle contracts; this is called animation and is normal. Your surgeon will advise which placement is appropriate for you.

What the operation involves

Before and after photographs should be taken for your clinical record, to help you and your surgeon plan the operation and assess the result. Your face is not included and you will be asked for consent; if your surgeon wants to use the images for teaching or publication, they must ask for specific additional consent.

Breast enlargement surgery takes about one-and-a-half hours and is usually done under general anaesthetic. You may be able to go home the same day, but many patients spend one night in hospital. Postoperative pain should be well controlled: your chest may feel tight and your breasts and ribs may be tender. You will be mobile from day one and should be back to full exercise within six weeks, with one to two weeks off work recommended.

At first the breasts may look high and the skin tight; this tends to settle over the first six weeks, but the long-term result takes three to four months as a more natural shape emerges. Most patients are pleased with their surgery, though some find the new shape difficult to get used to. Scars are typically quite red for the first six weeks, change to purple over the next three months and then fade to white. Most patients form good-quality scars, but abnormal scarring can occur.

Implant techniques

Choosing the implant

Choosing the implant
DecisionWhat the BAPRAS guide says
Fill materialThe outer shell of all implants is made of silicone, and some have an additional polyurethane coating. The shell is filled with either silicone gel or saline. Implants have been used since the 1960s and the evidence suggests they are safe. Most patients are offered silicone gel-filled implants — they tend to feel the most natural, come in a range of shapes and are durable. Saline implants feel less natural, folds or ripples may be more visible, and they carry a risk of deflation. All other filler materials have been withdrawn for use in the UK. Ask your surgeon exactly which type and manufacturer will be used, and why.
SizeImplants are supplied by volume, and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size. Your surgeon assesses your chest wall, your existing breast tissue and how much skin is available, then indicates an appropriate range — your own view matters, because in most patients a range of sizes could be used. The larger the implant and the slimmer you are, the less natural the result; an implant out of proportion with your frame is more likely to cause complications such as drooping, stretching of the breast tissue and being more easily felt.
ShapeImplants are round or teardrop (anatomical). Round implants give more volume at the top of the breast and are as wide as they are tall. With teardrop implants the width and height can be chosen separately, giving more control of the eventual shape. Both come in varying degrees of projection; your surgeon discusses the best shape for your frame and desired outcome.
TextureSurfaces are smooth or textured, in degrees from very fine to coarse; some implants have a foamy polyurethane coating. Texturing exists to reduce capsular contracture (evidence is strongest when the implant is placed in front of the muscle) and to reduce unwanted movement or rotation — so anatomical implants tend to be textured, while rotation of a round implant is not noticeable. A textured surface is linked to the uncommon BIA-ALCL; smooth implants currently have no such link. Smooth implants are almost always round, move within the breast and take several months to settle, and can slip sideways (lateral displacement) or drop below the crease (bottoming out). The choice is not straightforward — your surgeon should help decide.
Silicone safetyImplants are made from medical-grade silicone. Small quantities of silicone can be taken up by the body and found in breast tissue and sometimes the armpit lymph glands; occasionally the body forms inflammation and extra tissue around silicone deposits (silicone granuloma). If the shell fails, the gel often keeps its shape and the appearance may not change — ruptures are frequently discovered by accident while investigating another breast problem, though they can cause lumpiness or a change in shape. A confirmed rupture is treated by removal of the implants, with replacement possible at the same or a later operation. There is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer.

The three most important decisions are implant size, shape and placement. Summarised from the BAPRAS implant techniques guide.

What complications can occur?

All operations are associated with risks. Serious complications are uncommon with breast augmentation, occurring in less than 1 in 100 operations. The figures below are those published in the BAPRAS guide.

Reported frequencies

Risks and how often they occur

Risks and how often they occur
ComplicationWhat the BAPRAS guide says
Serious complications overallUncommon — less than 1 in 100 breast augmentation operations.
Bleeding (haematoma)Less than 1 in 100. Usually immediately after surgery, occasionally up to two weeks later. The breast becomes very swollen and tight and you return to theatre to have the blood removed and the bleeding stopped; the implant can be retained. Expect an extra night in hospital and more bruising than usual. Haematoma can increase the risk of later capsular contracture.
InfectionLess than 1 in 1000. Usually apparent over the first two or three weeks: swelling, tenderness, redness, wound discharge and a raised temperature. Antibiotics sometimes settle a mild infection, but most established infections around the implant require removal — a new implant cannot be inserted immediately, and three to six months should pass before re-insertion. Your package price should cover treatment of bleeding or infection.
Capsular contractureThe body forms a scar capsule around every implant; when it contracts the breast feels firmer, and may become round or tender. Noticeable firmness occurs in up to 1 in 10 of all breast augmentations, but most of those patients do not need revision surgery. Options include living with it (safe), releasing the capsule (capsulotomy) or removing it (capsulectomy) with a new implant — but scar tissue can return in at least half of people having secondary surgery. Capsular contracture is the most common reason for re-operation, and once it has happened it is likely to recur in 1 in 2 cases.
Re-operation for any reasonAbout 1% (1 in 100) per year — so after 10 years, about 10 in every 100 women will have had more surgery.
Changes in sensationSome alteration of sensation is usual, most often numbness and oversensitivity of the nipples. Oversensitivity gradually settles, usually over several months. Around 1 in 5 patients have a reduction in nipple sensation; recovery can take up to 12 months, and 1 in 10 patients have some permanent numbness.
Feeling or seeing the implantIt is common to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and does not improve with time. Ripples or folds may become visible leaning forwards. Small amounts of your own fat can be injected (lipomodelling) to improve the situation in some patients. A marked crease can be a sign of capsular contracture.
Implant failure (rupture)The shell can eventually fail. The American Core study (FDA update, 2011) found 1 in 10 implants had ruptured at 10 years, and it is estimated half of all breast implants may rupture by 15 years. Rupture is often contained within the body’s own capsule (silent rupture) and does not appear harmful; some patients notice a change in size, shape or consistency, a lump or swelling. A scan is usually performed and, if rupture is suggested, removal and exchange is advised. There is no universally agreed replacement schedule, and exchange before ten years is unusual — if you have noticed no change, no regular follow-up or scans are needed.
AsymmetrySome asymmetry between breasts is normal and perfect symmetry is not an achievable goal; asymmetry may appear more pronounced after surgery. A larger implant in the smaller breast improves the volume difference only, not other differences such as nipple position. Implants can also settle differently in their pockets.
Wide cleavageImplants are positioned centrally behind the nipples and will not improve a naturally wide cleavage — with sub-muscular placement the cleavage can even appear wider. Breasts and implants falling to the sides when you lie down is normal.
Stretch marks and veinsStretch marks may develop after surgery, especially with larger implants, and veins may become more noticeable on the breast surface.
Ptosis (sagging)Breasts will sag with time because augmented breasts are larger and heavier — the larger the implant, the more the breast will droop. They may also “bottom out”, meaning the implant sits lower, below the nipple rather than above it.
Pregnancy and breastfeedingImplants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed. There is some evidence that the amount of milk produced by some women with implants is reduced, and no evidence of increased illness in children of women with silicone gel implants. Pregnancy and breastfeeding may adversely affect the shape of the breast.
Other reasons for re-operationSome patients choose re-augmentation with larger implants as time goes by; augmented breasts change shape with time, pregnancy and weight fluctuation; teardrop-shaped implants can rotate behind the breast (usually rotating back by themselves or being gently pushed back, but repeated rotation needs re-operation, especially with large implants correcting droop); and intermittent swelling around an implant may lead to scans, further tests or implant replacement.
Who pays for future treatmentMany of these long-term problems will not be covered by the package bought at the time of surgery, and you should not expect the NHS to provide future treatment. You must be prepared to pay for consultations, scans and further surgery if needed.

Frequency figures are those published in the BAPRAS patient guide (updated 2021) and describe breast augmentation generally; individual risk depends on your anatomy, the technique used and your health.

Breast Implant Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL)

Since 2016, anaplastic large cell lymphoma in association with breast implants has been recognised by the World Health Organization. The risk is small. It is not a breast cancer but a type of cancer associated with the scar tissue (capsule) the body lays down around an implant. Cases have occurred between 2 and 28 years after implant insertion, with an average of 8 years, and it most likely presents as swelling around the implant (a seroma) causing an increase in breast size. It can usually be treated successfully by removing the implant and the surrounding capsule.

Because it is uncommon, international organisations share data on the condition. Most cases worldwide have occurred in women with textured breast implants, with higher numbers where the texture is coarser — so ask your surgeon for the most up-to-date recommendations. Breast implants continue to hold safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and the USA FDA and remain used in breast reconstruction after cancer worldwide.

Breast Implant Illness (BII)

Breast Implant Illness is a term used by some patients who experience symptoms they feel are connected to their silicone implants — tiredness, “brain fog”, joint aches, immune-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, depression, hormonal issues, headaches, hair loss, chills, rash and neurological issues. BII is not a medical diagnosis, there is no proven association with breast implants, and there is currently no scientific evidence confirming the proposed link or any diagnostic test for the condition; research continues. Some patients report improvement after implant removal, but not all do. The UK government guidance on BII symptoms and the FDA’s breast-implant risk pages are referenced in the guide.

Long-term consequences and alternatives

Mammography and screening

Implants push your natural breasts forward and do not make it harder to examine your breasts for lumps, but they do interfere with mammography: X-rays cannot pass through the implant, so some breast tissue is obscured. UK breast screening starts at age 50. If you are called for a screening mammogram you must tell the service you have implants — they may scan you at a different centre and take special views. The more of your total breast volume that is implant, the greater the problem, so a breast augmentation reduces the sensitivity of a future mammogram. Some patients pay privately for MRI screening instead to avoid these issues.

Myths and routine replacement

It is not unsafe to sunbathe or to fly in an aeroplane with implants — neither presents a problem. There is no need to massage breast implants, and this is not recommended with modern textured-surface implants. Routine replacement after a specified time is not recommended: replacement is advised only if you are unhappy with the appearance or have developed a problem.

Alternatives: lipofilling and breast uplift

The only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast is lipofilling (fat transfer): fat is removed by liposuction from the hips, thighs or tummy and injected into the breast area. Only a relatively small amount can be injected, so multiple operations are usually needed for a worthwhile effect; some fat is absorbed in the first weeks, but fat lasting beyond that brings permanent enlargement. It is more gradual than implant surgery and avoids an implant, but the surgeon cannot be sure how effective it will be and results are variable. Your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected into the breast — other materials have been tried and withdrawn. Do not allow anyone to inject anything other than your own fat.

If you are bothered by droopiness but happy with your breast size, you do not need an augmentation — you may be offered a breast uplift (mastopexy), which lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens the skin, with incisions around the areola and possibly vertically and under the breast. Scarring is more obvious than with augmentation alone and no implant is used, but uplifted breasts tend to droop again with time and gravity, and often seem smaller afterwards despite little or no tissue removal. Mild droopiness can be improved by augmentation alone; where both volume loss and droopiness are a problem, augmentation and mastopexy may be discussed as one operation or in two stages — usually best done one at a time, though sometimes performed together after careful planning and counselling, with results that are not always entirely predictable in size and shape.

Breast Implant Registry

In the UK there is a national Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry, administered by NHS Digital, recording every implant placed or removed with patient details, the organisation and the surgeon. Its main aim is to trace and inform affected patients if a failed implant is ever recalled, and to identify possible trends and complications relating to specific implants. Entry requires your consent, and you are strongly recommended to agree to the register if you have implant-based surgery — for your own protection and that of others.

Quick answers

Questions the BAPRAS guide answers

No. Implants are supplied by volume and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size. Your surgeon assesses your chest wall, existing breast tissue and available skin, then indicates an appropriate range of sizes — in most patients a range could be used, and your own preference decides where in that range to sit.

No. There is no universally agreed replacement schedule, and exchange before ten years is unusual. If you have noticed no change you do not need regular follow-up or scans. You should still be prepared — personally and financially — for further surgery at some point, since about 1% of patients have a re-operation each year.

Cosmetically, no — you would consult and pay as a private patient. Exceptions include very uneven breasts, having no breasts, or treatment within a reconstruction care plan. If you have surgery abroad, only emergency complications will be treated by the NHS on your return.

At least two weeks between your decision and surgery, plus an offer of a second consultation beforehand. Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation: if you are pressured to proceed or offered no cooling-off period, walk away.

Implants are made from medical-grade silicone and have been used since the 1960s; the evidence suggests they are safe, and there is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer. Rupture remains possible (about 1 in 10 at 10 years) and is usually treated by removal and exchange. Rare risks such as BIA-ALCL, and the symptoms described as breast implant illness, are covered above.

Lipofilling — transferring your own fat by liposuction and injection. It avoids an implant but usually needs several operations for a worthwhile effect, gives a gradual result and is variable. Your own fat is the only substance that should ever be injected into the breast.

This library collects the BAAPS’s public patient information on breast enlargement and the decisions around it — including the joint ABS, BAAPS and BAPRAS booklet Your Guide to Breast Augmentation. Every entry links to the original page or PDF on baaps.org.uk, so the wording, dates and any subsequent updates can be checked at source.

What this library does and does not mean

BAAPS is a professional association of aesthetic plastic surgeons; it publishes patient education and safety guidance but does not endorse any particular clinic, surgeon outside its membership, or treatment package. Nothing here is a recommendation to have a procedure, and individual suitability always requires assessment by a qualified clinician.

Summaries and key points are condensed from BAAPS pages and the joint patient booklet for readability. They are not a substitute for the original documents, which may have been updated since this library was compiled on 2026-10-20. Always read the current version on baaps.org.uk and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

Coverage

What the BAAPS information covers

The library is grouped into four areas, from the procedure itself to implant safety and consumer guidance.

The procedure

What breast augmentation involves, consultation and consent, implant placement, operation time, recovery and expected outcomes.

The patient booklet

The joint ABS, BAAPS and BAPRAS guide: decisions, costs, techniques, implant type, size, shape and texture, complications with frequencies, long-term consequences and alternatives.

Implant safety

Breast Implant Illness (BII), BIA-ALCL, BIA-SCC, PIP implants and the association’s published safety statements.

Consumer guidance

Fourteen safety points covering your own decision, research, questions, credentials, cooling-off periods, timing and taking your time.

Complications

Bleeding, infection, asymmetry, capsular contracture, sensation changes, palpability, rupture and revision rates with typical frequencies from the booklet.

Alternatives

Fat transfer (lipofilling) and breast uplift (mastopexy) as alternatives or adjuncts to implant augmentation, and the UK implant registry.

Breast augmentation

BAAPS patient information on breast enlargement itself: what the operation involves, consultation and consent, techniques, implant choices, recovery and expected outcomes.

Breast Augmentation

Procedure page · Updated 2021

The BAAPS procedure page for breast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation, BBA) — an operation to enlarge the breasts, usually by inserting an implant beneath the breast tissue. The page describes the procedure as potentially life-enhancing but stresses that it is a big decision, major surgery with potential risks, and that the hoped-for result cannot be guaranteed. It links to the full joint patient booklet and lists the common names patients use for the procedure.

  • Breast augmentation (BBA) is an operation to enlarge the breasts, usually by inserting an implant beneath the breast tissue.
  • It can be a life-enhancing procedure, but having a breast enlargement is a big decision.
  • It is major surgery with potential risks, and the result you may hope for cannot be guaranteed.
  • The joint ABS, BAAPS and BAPRAS booklet explains the procedure and the short- and long-term risks; any further questions after consultation should be asked of your surgeon.
  • The procedure is also commonly known as a boob job, enlargement, implant or breast size.

Your Guide to Breast Augmentation (ABS, BAAPS & BAPRAS, Edition 2, 2021)

Patient information booklet · Updated 2021-04

The joint patient booklet from the Association of Breast Surgery, BAAPS and BAPRAS. It covers who the guide is for and what breast augmentation involves; how to seek a consultation, check a surgeon's qualifications, understand costs and the cooling-off period; the surgery itself including implant placement (sub-glandular, sub-muscular, dual plane), operation time and recovery; implant type, size, shape and texture; a full list of complications with typical frequencies; long-term consequences including mammography, BIA-ALCL and breast implant illness; alternatives such as lipofilling and mastopexy; and the UK Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry. Editors: Lee Martin and Emma de Sousa; reviewed by PRASEAG.

  • Breast augmentation is usually done by inserting an implant beneath the breast to make it look larger; it can enlarge always-small breasts or fill out breasts that have emptied, for example after pregnancy.
  • It will reshape breasts to some extent and can also be used to correct unequal breast size.
  • Fat transfer (lipomodelling, lipofilling or fat grafting) is an alternative in a few people but is not suitable for all and often requires more than one episode of surgery.
  • Patients tend to be pleased with results, but you need realistic expectations and must understand what can and cannot be achieved, the limitations of surgery and the long-term consequences of implants.
  • Your initial consultation should be with the surgeon who will do the operation; your surgeon will normally seek permission to write to your GP; a consultation fee is normal.
  • At consultation you will be examined, measurements taken, and implant shapes, sizes and pocket positions discussed; some surgeons use implant sizers in a bra or 3D photography, which is only a guide — the same implant can look very different in different people.
  • You should be given a cooling-off period of at least two weeks before surgery and offered a second consultation; you should not feel rushed.
  • Breast augmentation is a lifetime commitment, not a one-stop permanent solution: you will need revision surgery as the years go by and must be prepared personally and financially.
  • Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation — if you are not offered a cooling-off period or are put under pressure, walk away.
  • Surgeons should be listed on the GMC specialist register (gmc-uk.org); membership of ABS, BAAPS and/or BAPRAS indicates a standard set of recognised qualifications.
  • Internet search listings may be promotional; a prominent listing measures marketing ability, not service quality.
  • Cosmetic breast augmentation is not available on the NHS except in exceptional circumstances such as very uneven breasts, no breasts, or as part of reconstruction; after surgery abroad the NHS will only deal with emergency complications on return.
  • Breast enlargement involves placing an implant under the breast tissue; implants are usually inserted through an incision under the breast at the crease, but can also go in via the armpit or around the nipple.
  • Implants can sit behind the breast on top of the chest wall muscle (sub-glandular) or behind the breast and muscle (sub-muscular); your surgeon will advise which is appropriate.
  • Sub-glandular placement is considered the simplest enlargement procedure and less likely to cause significant discomfort; it is also effective with some drooping.
  • Sub-muscular placement provides more padding for the implant, helpful for slender patients and those with little breast tissue, reducing the chances of feeling or seeing the implant.
  • Dual plane augmentation combines the two routes, placing implants partly behind the breast and partly behind the muscle; implants behind the muscle may move with muscle contraction (animation), which is normal.
  • Breast enlargement surgery takes about one-and-a-half hours, usually under general anaesthetic; you may go home the same day but many patients spend one night in hospital.
  • You will be mobile from day one and should be back to full exercise within six weeks; one to two weeks off work is recommended.
  • At first the breasts may look high and the skin tight; this tends to settle over the first six weeks, with the long-term result emerging over 3-4 months as a more natural shape appears.
  • Scars tend to be red in the first six weeks, change to purple over the next three months, then fade to white; abnormal scarring can occur.
  • All implant shells are made of silicone; some have an additional polyurethane coating; shells are filled with silicone gel or saline, and implants have been used since the 1960s with evidence suggesting they are safe.
  • Most patients are offered silicone gel-filled implants — they feel most natural, have a range of shapes and are durable; saline implants tend to feel less natural, ripples may be more visible and they carry a risk of deflation; all other filler materials have been withdrawn for use in the UK.
  • Implants are supplied by volume and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size; the larger the implant and the slimmer the patient, the less natural the result, and an out-of-proportion implant is more likely to cause drooping, tissue stretching and palpability.
  • Implants are round or teardrop-shaped (anatomical); round implants give bigger volume at the top and are the same width as tall, while teardrop implants allow width and height to be chosen separately; both come in varying degrees of projection.
  • Texturing reduces capsular contracture (particularly with implants placed in front of the muscle) and reduces movement or rotation; anatomical implants tend to be textured because rotation would alter the shape, while rotation of a round implant is not noticeable.
  • Textured surfaces are related to BIA-ALCL, an uncommon condition; smooth-surface implants currently appear to have no link to BIA-ALCL; smooth implants are almost always round and can take several months to settle, and may slip sideways (lateral displacement) or drop below the crease (bottoming out).
  • Small quantities of silicone from implants can be taken up by the body and found in breast tissue and sometimes armpit lymph glands; silicone granuloma is inflammation and extra tissue around silicone deposits.
  • Over time the implant shell may fail and gel may leak; many ruptures are discovered by accident, and a ruptured implant should be removed — replacement at the same or a later operation is a choice.
  • There is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer.
  • Serious complications are uncommon, occurring in less than 1 in 100 operations.
  • Bleeding (haematoma) occurs in less than 1 in 100, usually immediately but occasionally up to two weeks later; the breast becomes very swollen and tight and you return to theatre to have the blood removed — haematoma can increase the risk of later capsular contracture.
  • Infection occurs in less than 1 in 1000 cases, usually apparent over the first two or three weeks; most patients with an established infection around the implant need the implant removed, and a new implant cannot be inserted immediately — three to six months should wait for the infection to resolve.
  • Perfect symmetry is not an achievable goal; asymmetry can be of breast or nipple, size, shape and position, may appear more pronounced after surgery, and implants can settle differently in their pockets.
  • Some patients have a naturally wide cleavage that implants will not improve; with sub-muscular placement the cleavage can appear wider, and breasts and implants may fall to the sides when lying down, which is normal.
  • Stretch marks may develop, especially with larger implants, and veins may become more noticeable.
  • Breasts will sag with time because they are larger and heavier; the larger the implant, the more the breast will droop, and breasts may bottom out.
  • Implants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed, though some evidence suggests milk production may be reduced in some women; there is no evidence of increased illness in children of women with silicone gel implants.
  • Every patient forms a scar capsule around the implant; capsular contracture — when this scar contracts and makes the implant feel firmer — is up to 1 in 10 of all augmentations, but most of those patients will not need revision surgery.
  • About 1% (1 in 100) a year need re-operation for any reason, so after 10 years about 10% will have had more surgery; capsular contracture is the most common reason and is likely to recur in 1 in 2 cases after secondary surgery.
  • Around 1 in 5 patients will have reduced nipple sensation; recovery can take up to 12 months, but 1 in 10 will have some permanent numbness.
  • It is common to be able to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and will not improve with time; lipomodelling can improve the situation in some patients.
  • The American Core study (FDA Update 2011) suggested 1 in 10 implants had ruptured at 10 years, and half of all implants may rupture by 15 years; many ruptures are silent, contained within the capsule, and do not appear harmful.
  • There is no universally agreed replacement schedule for implants and it is unusual to need exchange before ten years; if you have noticed no change you do not need regular follow-up or scans — but you should be prepared personally and financially for possible future surgery.
  • Other reasons for re-operation include wanting larger implants, shape change with time or after pregnancy and weight fluctuation, rotation of teardrop implants, and intermittent swelling around implants.
  • Long-term problems will not usually be covered by the package bought at the time of augmentation, and the NHS should not be expected to provide future private treatment.
  • BIA-ALCL is recognised by the WHO as a condition associated with breast implants; it is not a breast cancer but a cancer of the scar tissue capsule, occurring between 2 and 28 years after insertion (average 8 years), usually presenting as swelling around the implant (seroma), and usually treated by removing the implant and capsule.
  • Most BIA-ALCL cases worldwide have occurred with textured implants, with higher numbers where the texture is coarser; breast implants continue to have safety approval from the MHRA and FDA and continue to be used in reconstruction worldwide.
  • Breast Implant Illness (BII) is a term used by some patients for symptoms including tiredness, brain fog, joint aches, immune-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, depression, hormonal issues, headaches, hair loss, chills, rash and neurological issues; it is not a medical diagnosis and there is no proven association with implants.
  • Some patients report symptoms improve if implants are removed, but this is not true for all; research continues.
  • Implants do not make breast self-examination more difficult, but they do interfere with mammography because X-rays cannot pass through the implant; tell the mammography service you have implants — special views or a different centre may be used, and some patients opt for private MRI screening.
  • It is safe to sunbathe and fly with implants; implant massage is not needed and is not recommended with modern textured implants; routine implant replacement after a specified time is not recommended.
  • The only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast is lipofilling: fat removed by liposuction from hips, thighs or tummy and injected into the breast; only a relatively small amount can be injected so multiple operations are needed for a worthwhile effect, and some fat is absorbed in the initial weeks — fat that lasts brings permanent enlargement.
  • Your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected into the breast; other materials have been tried and withdrawn — do not allow anyone to inject anything other than your own fat.
  • Breast uplift (mastopexy) is a different operation that lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens the skin without an implant; scarring is more obvious, and uplifted breasts tend to droop again with time and gravity.
  • Mild droopiness can be improved by augmentation alone, but where volume loss and droopiness both bother you, augmentation alone will not solve drooping — your surgeon should discuss augmentation with mastopexy, as one operation or in two stages.
  • In the UK the national Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry records all implants placed or removed, allowing patients to be traced in the event of a future recall and identification of trends; entry requires consent and is strongly recommended.
  • Avoid any deal with a non-refundable deposit or financial inducement to proceed — even refunding a consultation fee if you proceed with surgery is considered an inducement and against GMC guidance.
  • A package price covering the entire process and the cost of treating complications in the initial weeks is appropriate; the cheapest deal may not be the best.
  • Before your consultation it should be possible to obtain an approximate cost from your private hospital or the surgeon's secretary; after consultation(s) you should be given a written quote.

Breast implant safety

BAAPS information on breast implant associated conditions — Breast Implant Illness (BII), BIA-ALCL, BIA-SCC, PIP implants — and the association's published safety statements.

Breast Implant Safety

Safety information page

BAAPS information and guidance on breast implant associated conditions, with links to patient documents on Breast Implant Illness (BII) and BIA-ALCL, the association's updated BII statement of October 2022, joint statements on BIA-SCC and other breast implant associated lymphomas, PRASEAG guidance, the Allergan Natrelle textured implant withdrawal statement, the BAAPS/ABS/BAPRAS joint statement on breast implant safety, and BAAPS advice on PIP implants including signs and symptoms of rupture or inflammation.

  • BAAPS publishes patient documents on Breast Implant Illness (BII) and Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), plus an updated BII statement from October 2022.
  • In July 2023 BAAPS issued a joint statement on Breast Implant Associated Squamous Cell Carcinoma and other breast implant associated lymphomas.
  • PRASEAG issued a statement on breast implants and guidance for patients following MHRA advice on BIA-ALCL, with BAAPS, BAPRAS and the Association of Breast Surgery working together.
  • BAAPS issued statements on the withdrawal of Allergan (Natrelle) textured implants and a joint BAAPS/ABS/BAPRAS statement on breast implant safety (27 November 2018).
  • On PIP implants the 2013 expert group found no evidence they were responsible for an increased rate of breast cancer; the gel was less cohesive than most contemporary implants and had a greater potential to cause local inflammation on rupture.
  • Signs of PIP rupture, leak or inflammation include lumpiness of the breast, lumpiness or swelling of regional lymph nodes, change in shape and size, redness, tenderness, swelling and firmness; symptoms may include pain and hypersensitivity.
  • Patients unsure of their implant make should contact their surgeon or provider; patients with signs or symptoms of rupture or irritation should seek advice from their surgeon.
  • BAAPS advised removal or replacement of PIP implants as a precaution because of the inferior quality of the gel, regardless of rupture rate.
  • Breast implants continue to have safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and USA FDA and continue to be used in reconstruction worldwide.

Consumer safety guidelines

BAAPS fourteen-point consumer safety guidance for anyone considering aesthetic surgery, from making your own decision to checking credentials and taking your time.

BAAPS Consumer Safety Guidelines

Safety guidance

BAAPS fourteen-point consumer safety guidance for anyone considering aesthetic surgery: make your own decision, do your research, ask the right questions at every stage, know your surgeon and check credentials on the GMC specialist register, beware pressurising selling and non-refundable deposits, expect a two-week cooling-off period, get a second opinion if needed, time the surgery well, think about location and travel, talk to your GP, remember you can change your mind, use common sense about special offers, and take your time.

  • Only you can decide whether to go ahead with aesthetic surgery, but you need specialist input to understand what is possible, suitable and the risks and benefits.
  • No procedure is 100% risk free and no surgeon can give a 100% guarantee of results; research the limitations and risks before any consultation.
  • Know what will happen at every stage — pre-operative assessment, the day of surgery, aftercare, recovery time, follow-up and the possibility of further procedures.
  • Your consultation should be with the actual surgeon who will operate; clinic managers and nurses should not be your only point of contact.
  • A specialist plastic surgeon should have the FCRS (Plast) qualification and be listed on the Specialist Register of Plastic Surgeons with the GMC.
  • Avoid any marketing or selling technique that financially or temporally traps you, including booking fees and non-refundable advances; your decision should be free of incentive.
  • You should expect a two-week cooling-off period following your consultation to consider your options.
  • Get a second opinion if necessary; a reputable surgeon will never apply a time limit, withhold key information or upsell additional surgery.
  • Avoid surgery around major life events such as moving house, changing job, bereavement, relationship breakdown or the arrival of children.
  • Give careful consideration to travelling long distances or overseas for surgery; travel insurance often will not cover treatment or extra nights for elective aesthetic procedures.
  • Your GP can offer unbiased advice with no vested interest and may discuss functional, psychological and social benefits.
  • You can cancel right up until the time you go to sleep for surgery.
  • Don't be tempted by special offers or rushed into a quick surgery slot; anything that seems too good to be true probably is.
  • Take as much time as you need after an initial consultation; a surgeon might recommend two consultations before booking a procedure.

Source and copyright

BAAPS patient information describes practice in the United Kingdom; costs, funding, professional registration and clinical standards differ between countries, and local standards still apply where a procedure is performed. Cosmetic breast augmentation is generally private in the UK; the NHS may fund it only in exceptional circumstances.

The joint booklet Your Guide to Breast Augmentation is published by the Association of Breast Surgery, BAAPS and BAPRAS (Edition 2, BAPRAS London, 2021; editors Lee Martin and Emma de Sousa; reviewed by PRASEAG). This library stores only summaries, extracted facts and links to publicly available BAAPS pages and PDFs; BAAPS content remains the property of BAAPS and the respective publishing bodies.

For US regulator guidance, see the FDA information library. For UK health-service guidance, see the NHS information library. For academic patient education, see the Cleveland Clinic information library. For published research, see the PMC research library.

StatPearls reviews are educational clinical summaries, not guidelines, and they do not recommend any clinic, surgeon or treatment package. This page stores only paraphrased summaries, extracted facts and links: it is not a substitute for reading the original review, which may have been updated since it was captured on 2026-10-20. The review is grouped here into four themes, matching the sections of the original article.

Background
