Background and anatomy

What breast augmentation is, why it is performed, how the FDA has treated silicone implants over time, and the anatomy the operation works on. (3)

Continuing Education Activity

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The review's opening summary: breast augmentation increases breast size, most often with an implant and less commonly with fat transfer, and is among the most commonly performed plastic surgery procedures in the United States. It frames the activity around indications, contraindications, complications and the role of the interprofessional team before and after surgery.

  • Objectives are to identify the different techniques, describe the indications, review the complications and improve care coordination among the team.
  • The FDA restricted silicone-filled implants for cosmetic enhancement from 1992; reconstructive patients continued to receive them after mastectomy.
  • The activity is written for the interprofessional team involved in pre- and postoperative care.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Introduction

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure in which breast size is enhanced, either by placing an implant or, less commonly, through fat transfer. The section traces FDA policy on silicone implants from the 1992 restriction to the 2006 reversal, describes the shift towards cohesive gel and form-stable implants, and sets out monitoring advice and the fact that implants are not permanent devices.

  • Extensive research failed to confirm the disease fears that led to the 1992 silicone restriction, and the FDA allowed general use of silicone-filled implants again in 2006.
  • By 2017 the majority of patients undergoing augmentation received cohesive gel silicone implants, with makers introducing different levels of gel firmness.
  • The FDA recommends MRI screening every two years in patients with silicone implants to detect subclinical leaks, but adherence is incomplete and MRI readings can be false positive.
  • Higher gel cohesion may lower rupture rates, but the review states that eventually all implants will rupture or break.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Anatomy and Physiology

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The anatomy relevant to augmentation: the breast sits on the anterior chest wall below the clavicle, bounded medially by the sternum, laterally by the latissimus dorsi and inferiorly by the inframammary fold, with the pectoralis muscles forming its posterior boundary.

  • The inframammary fold is a dermal structure formed by fusion of the superficial and mammary fascia.
  • Blood supply comes from the subdermal plexus with major contributions from the internal mammary artery, external mammary artery and intercostal perforators.
  • Nerve supply is mainly through the intercostal plexus, with most contribution from the third to fifth intercostal nerves.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Indications and contraindications

Who the review says the procedure is for, and the conditions that should stop a surgeon from operating. (2)

Indications

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Implants are placed for reconstruction after mastectomy, for developmental disorders such as hypomastia, and for elective reasons related to self-image. Hypomastia may follow normal development or involution, especially after pregnancy, and people of all personality types may seek the procedure.

  • Reported motivations include reconstruction, developmental under-development of the breast and elective enhancement of self-image.
  • The review notes that when surveyed after surgery, the vast majority of women would undergo the operation again.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Contraindications

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Most patients have no contraindications, but the review lists the conditions that should prevent surgery and the patient factors that should pause it.

  • Absolute reasons not to operate include active infection of the breast, active cancer and pregnancy.
  • Relative reasons include a history of autoimmune disease, current radiation treatment, unstable medical conditions and known sensitivity to silicone.
  • Psychological instability or unrealistic expectations are also given as reasons not to proceed.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

The operation

Equipment, theatre team, preparation, implant choices, placement, incisions, anaesthesia, duration and expected recovery. (4)

Equipment

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Routine operating-room equipment is usually sufficient. Extras depend on the approach: a lighted retractor or headlight for visualising the pocket, an endoscope for umbilical or axillary approaches, and sometimes an implant sleeve used as part of a no-touch technique.

  • A no-touch technique limits handling of the implant to reduce implant trauma and bacterial contamination.
  • Endoscopic equipment may be required when the umbilical or axillary route is used.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Personnel

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The operating team normally consists of the surgeon, a scrubbed assistant, an anaesthesiologist and a circulating nurse working together in the operating room.

  • Standard theatre roles apply: surgeon, scrubbed assistant, anaesthesiologist and circulating nurse.
  • The team structure is described as the same as for other routine surgical procedures.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Preparation

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Patients are prepared for surgery as for any other surgical procedure, following the usual preoperative pathway.

  • Preparation follows the routine preoperative work-up used for any operation, including assessment and consent.
  • The review places emphasis on informed consent and on the pre-operative teaching that reduces later problems.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Technique or Treatment

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Two main implant types are described, saline-filled and silicone-filled, both with a silicone outer shell that can be smooth or textured. Implants can sit above or beneath the pectoralis muscle, be reached through inframammary, transaxillary or peri-areolar incisions, and are usually done as an outpatient operation under general anaesthesia.

  • Saline implants are inserted empty and filled through a port, typically with a 25 to 50 mL range specified by the manufacturer.
  • Saline implants are FDA-approved from age 18 for augmentation and at any age for reconstruction; silicone gel implants are approved from age 22.
  • Silicone implants suit patients with thin soft-tissue coverage better, showing less rippling and a softer, more natural feel.
  • Texturing prevents rotation in shaped implants and may lower capsular contracture in the subglandular pocket, but not in the submuscular pocket.
  • No single placement method is uniformly accepted as best; the choice is made jointly by patient and surgeon.
  • The operation generally takes 45 to 90 minutes; most patients return to light work within a week, with full activity taking up to six weeks.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Complications and outcomes

Early and late complications, capsular contracture, implant longevity, reported satisfaction and how the care team reduces risk. (4)

Complications

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Complication rates are described as low, but no implant is a lifetime device. Early problems include infection, bleeding and sensory change; later problems include malposition, deflation or leak and capsular contracture, which may require further surgery.

  • Surgeons commonly estimate a 15 to 20 year lifespan for implants, with no uniform recommendation on routine replacement.
  • Early complications listed are infection, scarring, asymmetry, haematoma, seroma, breast pain, poor cosmetic outcome and changes in nipple or breast sensation.
  • Later complications listed are implant malposition or displacement, implant deflation or leak, and capsular contracture.
  • Capsular contracture is graded 1 to 4 and may require surgical correction or implant removal when severe.
  • Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes are the microorganisms most commonly isolated in studies of capsular contracture, supporting a suspected biofilm or low-grade infection mechanism.
  • A slim possibility of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is reported, possibly linked to a particular type of implant texturing, although the exact relationship is not yet determined.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Clinical Significance

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

The procedure remains highly popular, and the review stresses that clinicians treating women with implants should be aware of them, because the implants are relevant to other conditions and to screening.

  • The American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported approximately 290,000 augmentation procedures performed in the United States in 2016.
  • The vast majority of patients report improved self-esteem and satisfaction with the decision.
  • Doctors treating these patients for other conditions should have an awareness of the procedure and of implants in general.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes

StatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18

Risk reduction is described as a team effort: informed consent, nurse-led preoperative instruction, smoking cessation, pharmacist medicines checks and early recognition of problems. Outcomes are reported as good, with most patients pleased with the result.

  • Many past litigations arose primarily from a lack of informed consent, which the pre-operative visit is meant to address.
  • Patients should be instructed to stop smoking and make positive lifestyle changes so results last longer.
  • Pharmacists contribute by checking allergies and explaining medicines, which can reduce infection and help pain control.
  • Surveys cited in the review indicate about 70 to 80 percent of patients are satisfied and feel the outcome was perfect.

Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →

What this library does and does not mean

MedlinePlus is a consumer-health information service of the U.S. National Library of Medicine. It does not provide medical advice, endorse any clinic, surgeon or treatment package, or approve breast enlargement as a procedure. Nothing here is a recommendation to have a treatment, and individual suitability can only be assessed in a consultation.

Summaries and key points are condensed from MedlinePlus pages for readability. They are not a substitute for the original documents, which may have been updated since this library was compiled on 2026-10-20. Always read the current version on medlineplus.gov and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

Breast augmentation surgery

The MedlinePlus encyclopedia article on the operation itself: what it is, how implants are placed, the anaesthetic and incision options, why it is performed, and the full risk list.

Breast augmentation surgery

Medical Encyclopedia article · Page last reviewed 2025-02-17

The MedlinePlus overview of breast augmentation: enlarging or reshaping the breasts by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or under the chest muscle fascia. The article covers the two implant fills (sterile saline and silicone), the outpatient or hospital setting, general versus local anaesthetic, the four usual incision routes, how implant and technique choices affect pain, appearance, implant integrity and future mammograms, the reasons for surgery, the risks (including capsular contracture, implant rupture, breast implant-associated lymphoma and reported systemic symptoms), what to arrange before the operation, what happens afterwards, and the expected outcome.

  • Augmentation is done by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or beneath the chest muscle, and implants are sacs filled with either sterile salt water or silicone.
  • The operation is performed at an outpatient surgery clinic or in a hospital, most often under general anaesthetic, with local anaesthetic as an alternative.
  • Four incision routes are described: the natural fold under the breast (the most common), the armpit using an endoscope, the edge of the areola, and, for saline implants only, a route near the navel through which the empty implant is tunnelled and then filled.
  • An areola-edge incision may bring more difficulty with breastfeeding and more loss of nipple sensation, and may carry a higher risk of capsular contracture.
  • Implant type, implant size and the chosen operation influence post-operative pain, the appearance achieved, the chance of later breakage or leakage, and the extra views future mammograms will need.
  • Reasons for the procedure include increasing breast size, changing breast shape and correcting a congenital deformity; patients are told to expect improvement rather than perfection.
  • Risks shared with any operation are listed as reactions to medicines, breathing problems, bleeding, blood clots and infection.
  • Breast-specific risks include difficulty breastfeeding, numbness around the nipple or surrounding skin, small or thickened raised scars, uneven nipple position, differences in size or shape between the two breasts, implant breakage or leakage, visible rippling, infection requiring implant removal, the need for more breast surgery and puncture of the lung.
  • A capsule of scar tissue normally forms around a new implant; when it thickens it can change the breast's shape, harden the breast tissue or cause pain.
  • A rare immune-system cancer, breast implant-associated lymphoma, has been reported with some implants, presenting as a mass or swelling around the implant with breast pain and treated by removing the implant and the tissue around it.
  • Some people report systemic symptoms after implants — grouped under breast implant illness, which the page says is not yet established as a recognised illness — including fatigue, memory and concentration problems, joint and muscle pain, anxiety, hair loss, depression, rash, autoimmune disease, inflammation and weight change; some improve after removal and some do not.
  • Before surgery patients should ask about a screening mammogram, disclose any pregnancy possibility and every medicine or supplement they take, review diabetes, heart disease and other conditions, stop smoking (which slows healing and raises clot risk), prepare the home and arrange transport and help for one to two days.
  • During the week before surgery, blood thinners such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen and vitamin E are commonly paused on the surgeon's advice, and fasting and morning-medicine instructions come from the surgical team.
  • Afterwards the breasts are wrapped in bulky gauze or a surgical bra, drainage tubes are removed within about three days, and massaging from around day five may be suggested to reduce capsular hardening after checking with the provider.
  • Outcomes are usually very good, scars are permanent and most visible during the first year before fading, a supportive bra may be worn for a few months, and later tests may be advised to confirm the implants are intact.

Recovery, discharge and wound care

Patient instructions for the days and weeks after cosmetic breast surgery, plus general guidance for looking after a surgical incision that has been left open.

Cosmetic breast surgery - discharge

Patient instructions · Page last reviewed 2025-02-17

Home-care instructions after cosmetic breast surgery — augmentation, lift or reduction. It covers what happens in hospital, what to expect once home, activity and driving limits, dressing and wound care, pain medicines and general self-care, and the symptoms that should prompt a call to the surgical team.

  • Surgery is done under general or local anaesthetic and takes an hour or more; patients wake with a gauze dressing or surgical bra and may have drainage tubes in place.
  • Most people go home the same day, though some stay one to two nights in hospital.
  • Pain, bruising and swelling are normal and settle over days to weeks, and reduced sensation in the breast skin or nipple may return gradually.
  • Short walks are encouraged early to support circulation; returning to work or other activities commonly takes 7 to 14 days or longer.
  • Heavy lifting, strenuous exercise and overstretching the arms are avoided for 3 to 6 weeks, and driving should wait at least two weeks and until drowsiness-inducing pain medicines have stopped.
  • Drainage tubes are removed at a visit within a few days and stitches within two weeks; surgical glue dissolves on its own and does not need removing.
  • Dressings stay in place as instructed, incisions are kept clean, dry and covered, and are checked daily for redness, pain or drainage.
  • Once dressings are no longer needed, a soft wireless supportive bra is worn day and night for 2 to 4 weeks; bathing is limited to showering after drains come out, with baths, hot tubs and swimming deferred until stitches and drains are out and the surgeon agrees.
  • Scars may take several months to more than a year to fade, and sunblock of SPF 30 or higher is advised whenever the scars are exposed.
  • Smoking is not permitted because it slows healing and raises the risk of complications and infection; alcohol is avoided while taking narcotic pain medicines, and aspirin, ibuprofen and other medicines or supplements need the surgeon's approval.
  • The surgeon should be contacted for increasing pain, redness, swelling, yellow or green drainage, bleeding or bruising at the incision, medicine side effects, a temperature of 100°F (38°C) or higher, numbness, loss of motion, or sudden swelling of the breast.

Read the original on medlineplus.gov →

Surgical wound care - open

Patient instructions · Page last reviewed 2026-01-01

General MedlinePlus instructions for looking after a surgical incision that has broken open and is being left to heal rather than re-closed with stitches. It explains healing from the inside out, hand hygiene before dressing changes, removing and replacing dressings, cleaning and irrigating the wound, disposal of used supplies, and the signs that mean a call to the provider. The breast augmentation article links this page for wound care after breast surgery.

  • A wound left open heals from the inside out, and the dressing absorbs drainage so the surface skin does not close before the tissue underneath has filled in.
  • Hands should be washed before every dressing change — an alcohol cleanser, or soap and water for 15 to 30 seconds including under the nails, with jewellery removed.
  • The skin around the wound is cleaned with saline or mild soapy water; alcohol, peroxide, iodine and antibacterial cleansers are avoided because they can damage wound tissue and slow healing.
  • Where irrigation is advised, a syringe of saline or soapy water is held about 2.5 to 15 cm from the wound to wash away discharge, then the area is patted dry.
  • No lotion, cream or herbal remedy goes on or near the wound without the provider's agreement; dressings are used once only and soiled material is bagged before disposal.
  • Contact the provider for more redness, pain, swelling or bleeding, a wound that looks larger, deeper, dried out or dark, thicker or foul-smelling discharge, or a temperature of 100.5°F (38°C) or higher.

It summarises the body areas people most often have reshaped — including increasing, reducing or reshaping sagging breasts — and links out to the encyclopedia articles and image series, the breast lift video, ASPS plastic surgery statistics, ClinicalTrials.gov searches for breast implants and plastic surgery, and patient handouts including the breast augmentation article in this library.

  • Breast surgery appears among the most commonly requested cosmetic changes: enlarging, reducing or reshaping sagging breasts.
  • The page indexes the breast augmentation, lift and reduction encyclopedia articles, their image series and the breast lift anatomy video.
  • It links to FDA breast implant information, American Society of Plastic Surgeons statistics and ClinicalTrials.gov searches for breast implants and plastic surgery procedures.
  • English and Spanish versions exist for the topic page and most of the linked resources.

Key facts from the MedlinePlus pages

The statements below summarise what MedlinePlus says about breast enlargement and the decisions around it. The right-hand column links to the source page.

Key facts from the MedlinePlus pages
TopicWhat MedlinePlus saysSource
What breast augmentation isMedlinePlus describes breast augmentation as a procedure to enlarge the breasts or change their shape, carried out by placing an implant behind the breast tissue or under the muscle fascia or chest muscle.Breast augmentation surgery
Implant fillsAn implant is a sac filled with either sterile salt water (saline) or a material called silicone.Breast augmentation surgery
Setting and anaestheticThe operation is done at an outpatient surgery clinic or in a hospital, with most women receiving general anaesthesia while local anaesthesia — staying awake with the breast area numbed — is an alternative.Breast augmentation surgery
Incision routesFour approaches are described: a cut in the natural fold under the breast (the most common technique), a cut under the arm often using an endoscope (leaving no scar on the breast but possibly one under the arm), a cut around the areola edge, and, for saline implants, a cut near the navel through which the implant is moved up and filled.Breast augmentation surgery
Areola-edge trade-offsThe periareolar route may bring more problems with breastfeeding and loss of sensation around the nipple, and may carry a higher risk of capsular contracture.Breast augmentation surgery
What changes the resultThe type of implant, its size and the type of surgery affect post-operative pain, the appearance of the breast, the risk of the implant breaking or leaking later, and the additional views future mammograms will require.Breast augmentation surgery
Why it is performedThe procedure is carried out to increase breast size, to change breast shape, or to correct a congenital deformity, with patients advised to discuss realistic expectations — improvement rather than perfection.Breast augmentation surgery
General surgical risksRisks applying to anaesthesia and surgery in general include reactions to medicines, breathing problems, bleeding, blood clots and infection.Breast augmentation surgery
Breast surgery risksListed breast risks include difficulty breastfeeding, loss of feeling in the nipple area or surrounding skin, small or thickened raised scars, uneven nipple position, differences in size or shape between the breasts, breaking or leakage of the implant, visible rippling, removal of the implant because of infection, the need for further breast surgery and puncture of the lung.Breast augmentation surgery
Capsular contractureA capsule of scar tissue normally forms around a new implant to hold it in place; if this capsule thickens and grows it can change the breast's shape, harden breast tissue or cause pain.Breast augmentation surgery
Breast implant-associated lymphomaA rare lymphoma of the immune system has been reported with some implant types, presenting as a mass or swelling around the implant together with breast pain, and treated by removing the implant and the tissue around it; research into other cancer links is ongoing.Breast augmentation surgery
Breast implant illnessSome people report systemic symptoms after receiving implants — fatigue, memory and concentration problems, joint and muscle pain, anxiety, hair loss, depression, rash, autoimmune disease, inflammation and weight gain or loss — described as breast implant illness, which the page says does not yet have enough evidence to be a recognised illness; some report improvement after implant removal and others do not.Breast augmentation surgery
Overall safety statementDespite these rare risks, MedlinePlus states that breast implants are considered safe.Breast augmentation surgery
Screening before surgeryPatients are advised to ask whether a screening mammogram is needed given their age and breast cancer risk, arranged early enough that any further imaging or biopsy cannot delay the planned operation.Breast augmentation surgery
What to tell the surgeonThe surgeon or nurse should be told about any pregnancy or possibility of pregnancy and about every medicine, drug, supplement or herb being taken, including items bought without a prescription.Breast augmentation surgery
Medical conditions and smokingDiabetes, heart disease and other conditions may require review by the provider who treats them, and smoking should be cut down or stopped because it slows healing and raises the risk of blood clots — surgery may be postponed while smoking continues.Breast augmentation surgery
Blood thinners before surgeryDuring the week before surgery, medicines that stop blood clotting — including over-the-counter aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen and vitamin E as well as many prescription medicines — are commonly stopped temporarily on the surgeon's advice, with instructions on which medicines to still take on the day of surgery.Breast augmentation surgery
Day-of-surgery instructionsOn the day of surgery patients follow the rules given about when to stop eating and drinking, take only the prescribed medicines with a small sip of water, and arrive at the hospital at the requested time.Breast augmentation surgery
Immediately after surgeryMost patients go home once the anaesthetic has worn off and they can walk, drink water and use the bathroom safely; the breasts are wrapped in a bulky gauze dressing or a surgical bra, and drainage tubes, if placed, are removed within 3 days.Breast augmentation surgery
Massage after surgeryMassaging the breasts from about 5 days after surgery may be recommended to reduce hardening of the capsule around the implant, but should only begin after checking with the provider.Breast augmentation surgery
Outcome and follow-upOutcomes from breast surgery are usually very good, pain and skin symptoms from the surgery generally settle, a special supportive bra may be worn for a few months, scars are permanent but typically fade after being most visible in the first year, and future tests may be recommended to confirm the implants have not ruptured.Breast augmentation surgery
Activity after dischargeHome instructions after cosmetic breast surgery allow short walks early, put return to work or other activity at 7 to 14 days or longer, and prohibit heavy lifting, strenuous exercise and overstretching the arms for 3 to 6 weeks, with driving delayed at least 2 weeks.Cosmetic breast surgery - discharge
Signs to call the surgeonThe surgical team should be contacted for increasing pain, redness, swelling, yellow or green drainage, bleeding or bruising at the incision, medicine side effects, a fever of 100°F (38°C) or higher, numbness or loss of motion, or sudden swelling of the breast.Cosmetic breast surgery - discharge
Scar care after dischargeIncision scars may take several months to more than a year to fade, and protecting them with sunblock of SPF 30 or higher is advised whenever they are exposed to the sun.Cosmetic breast surgery - discharge
Healing an open incisionWhere an incision has broken open and is not re-closed, healing proceeds from the inside out and a dressing absorbs drainage so the surface does not close over before the wound underneath has filled in.Surgical wound care - open
Cleansers to avoidSaline or mild soapy water is used to clean around the wound, while skin cleansers, alcohol, peroxide, iodine and antibacterial soaps are avoided because they can damage wound tissue and slow healing.Surgical wound care - open
Wound infection warningsA provider should be contacted if redness, pain, swelling or bleeding increases, the wound looks larger, deeper, dried out or dark, discharge becomes thicker or smells of pus, or temperature reaches 100.5°F (38°C).Surgical wound care - open
Scope of the topic pageThe MedlinePlus Plastic and Cosmetic Surgery topic page lists increasing, reducing and reshaping sagging breasts among the most common cosmetic requests and indexes the breast augmentation, lift and reduction articles, image series and video.Plastic and Cosmetic Surgery

Coverage

What the Wikipedia article covers

A short article with a definition, four methods, one ineffective method, a see-also list and seven references.

Definition and context

Breast enlargement as natural mammoplasia or active intervention, and why breasts matter to self-image, femininity and sexual attractiveness.

Surgical method

Breast augmentation with implants or fat transfer, listed as an actual and potential method and linked to the augmentation articles.

Hormonal method

Pharmacological or hormonal enhancement with medications such as estrogen or breast enlargement supplements, with three supporting citations.

Food energy and KLF14

Increasing food energy intake to add adipose tissue near the breast area, with distribution between individuals controlled by the KLF14 gene.

Mechanical method

Mechanical breast enhancement, cited to a 2007 study of the Brava external tissue expander.

Ineffective methods

The Mark Eden bust developer, named and described as a fraudulently marketed method and device.

The article in brief

Breast enlargement is the enlargement of the breasts. It may occur naturally as in mammoplasia or may occur artificially through active intervention. Many women regard their breasts, which are female secondary sex characteristics, as important to their sexual attractiveness, as a sign of femininity that is important to their sense of self. Due to this, when a woman considers her breasts deficient in some respect, she might choose to engage in some activity intended to enhance them.

Mammoplasia. The article names natural breast enlargement as mammoplasia, distinguishing it from enlargement produced by active intervention.

Methods listed

Methods the article lists to achieve larger breasts

The four actual and potential methods named in the article, with the wording condensed from the source. The right-hand column points to the article’s own references.

Methods the article lists to achieve larger breasts
MethodCategoryWhat the article saysRefs
Surgical breast augmentationSurgicalThe article lists surgical breast augmentation as an actual and potential method to achieve larger breasts, naming two routes: breast implants and fat transfer (fat grafting). It links to the breast augmentation and breast implant articles for the operative detail, cost and risk information held there.—
Pharmacological or hormonal breast enhancementHormonalThe article lists pharmacological or hormonal breast enhancement through administration of medications such as estrogen or breast enlargement supplements. Three of the article's seven citations support this method: two clinical texts on hormone therapy and breast cancer metastasis, and a 1998 study on hormonal breast augmentation and insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I).[2] [3] [4]
Increasing food energy intakeWeight and body compositionThe article states that by increasing food energy intake, more adipose tissue will be created, part of which will consist of adipose tissue located near the breast area. The amount added to the breasts varies from person to person and is controlled by the KLF14 gene. The article notes that additional modification of the KLF14 gene can thus make sure even more of the adipose tissue increase will occur at the breasts.[5] [6]
Mechanical breast enhancementMechanical / externalThe article lists mechanical breast enhancement as a potential method, supported by a single citation: a 2007 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery study evaluating the Brava external tissue expander and asking whether breast enlargement without surgery is a reality.[7]

The article frames every prosthetic-breast placement under one of three purposes.

The three therapeutic purposes
PurposeWhat the article says

All sections captured from the article

Grouped by topic. Each entry gives a short summary, the main extracted points and a direct link to that section of the Wikipedia article.

Breast-implant prostheses

The four types of prosthesis the article describes, the history of each technology and the five generations of silicone-gel design.

Saline breast prosthesis

Article section

The history, surgical handling and cosmetic trade-offs of salt-water-filled implants.

  • First commercial saline prosthesis presented by Laboratoires Arion (France) in 1964.
  • Inserted empty through a short incision, then filled with saline and contoured for symmetry.
  • Good-to-excellent size and contour results, but rippling can show in women with little breast tissue.
  • With ample breast tissue and submuscular placement, results match those of silicone-gel implants.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Silicone-gel breast prosthesis

Article section

Five generations of silicone-gel implant design, from the 1963 Cronin–Gerow teardrop to today's cohesive gel.

  • Invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin; manufactured by Dow Corning; first used in 1962.
  • Second-generation thin shells proved fragile, with higher rupture, leakage and capsular contracture rates.
  • Polyurethane coating reduced contracture but was dropped in the U.S. over TDA, a carcinogenic breakdown product; still used in Europe and South America.
  • Fifth-generation semi-solid cohesive gel reduces leakage and migration, with lower contracture and rupture rates in 2004–2005 studies.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Alternative-composition breast prosthesis

Article section

Historic fillers — soy oil, polypropylene string, cartilage, wool, rubber, Teflon-silicone — described as harmful and discontinued.

  • Listed as the third category of prosthetic breast.
  • The article describes these filler substances as harmful to the woman's body.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Structured breast prosthesis

Article section

Nested saline-filled shells approved in 2014 in the U.S. and Canada; now discontinued.

  • Approved by the FDA (U.S.) and Health Canada in 2014.
  • Three nested silicone-rubber shells; saline fills the two spaces between them.
  • Inserted folded and empty, then filled with saline in the pocket.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Surgical technique

The three therapeutic purposes, the five surgical incisions and the four implant-pocket placements.

Types of surgical incision

Article section

Five incision routes for placing a prosthesis: inframammary, periareolar, transaxillary, transumbilical and transabdominal.

  • Inframammary gives the best access; periareolar is short but raises contracture and duct/nerve risks.
  • Transaxillary, TUBA and TABA routes avoid scarring the breast skin.
  • Incision choice shapes scar visibility, access, and breastfeeding risk.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Implant-pocket placement

Article section

Four placements relative to the pectoralis major muscle: subglandular, subfascial, subpectoral (dual plane) and submuscular.

  • Subglandular is closest to the natural plane but more prone to rippling in thin tissue.
  • Dual-plane (subpectoral) covers the upper implant with muscle while letting the lower half expand — with some risk of animation deformity.
  • Submuscular places the implant fully under the muscle without releasing its lower origin.
  • A 2026 series of 198 dual-plane II patients reported 1.0% revisions for superior malposition and 0.5% delayed mastopexy.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Recovery and complications

Post-surgical recovery, general medical complications, implant rupture, capsular contracture, revision surgery and systemic sickness.

Post-surgical recovery

Article section

Scar healing, return to normal activities and exercise limits after augmentation mammoplasty.

  • Scars heal at about 6 weeks and fade over several months, depending on skin type.
  • Most patients resume normal daily activities at about 1 week after surgery.
  • Submuscular placement means longer convalescence and more pain, because chest muscles were cut.
  • No exercise or strenuous activity for about six weeks; gentle arm movement is encouraged early.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Medical complications

Article section

Surgical risks and breast-specific complications, including reported rates and the 2019 Allergan recall.

  • Usual surgical risks: adverse anaesthetic reaction, haematoma, seroma and wound infection.
  • Breast-specific complications: pain, altered sensation, wrinkling or asymmetry, skin thinning, impeded breastfeeding and symmastia.
  • Implant surgery and tissue-expander complications occur in about 6–7% of patients.
  • By 10 years, about 20% of aesthetic and 50% of reconstruction patients needed explantation of a failed prosthesis.
  • In 2019 the FDA recalled all Allergan Biocell textured implants over BIA-ALCL, a lymphoma linked to their surface.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Rupture of the prosthetic breast

Article section

How the body's fibrous capsule can compress an implant until it ruptures, intracapsularly or extracapsularly, and how rupture is detected.

  • The immune system encases any implant in a collagen capsule; thickening can compress and rupture it.
  • Intracapsular rupture keeps filler inside the capsule; extracapsular rupture lets it migrate into the thorax, causing granulomas or lymphadenopathy.
  • Rupture is often unnoticed at first because saline and silicone gel are biologically inert.
  • Causes include surgical damage, later thoracic surgery, shell degradation, trauma and mechanical pressure such as capsular contracture or mammography.
  • Manual examination detects about 30% of ruptures; MRI detects about 86%.
  • The FDA advises an MRI at 3 years after surgery, then every two years for suspected rupture.
  • Reported saline rates: 3–5% rupture at 3 years and 7–10% at 10 years; ~10–13% overfilling cut the 8-year deflation rate to 1.83%.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Capsular contracture

Article section

The scar capsule tightening around an implant until it deforms or breaks the device — causes, prevention and treatment, plus revision surgery.

  • Causes include bacterial contamination, shell rupture, filler leakage and haematoma.
  • Lower contracture rates are associated with submuscular placement, textured surfaces, minimal implant handling and antibiotic irrigation.
  • Treatment ranges from open capsulotomy with implant replacement to non-surgical options (massage, ultrasound, leukotriene inhibitors, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy).
  • Indications for revision surgery: complications, capsular contracture, shell rupture, gel leakage and rupture-and-deflation.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Systemic sickness

Article section

Study evidence on whether silicone-gel implants cause systemic or autoimmune disease — consistently no causal link found.

  • Reviews since the 1990s report no causal relation to systemic or autoimmune disease, though some women report neurological and rheumatological symptoms.
  • A 2004 Danish study found no higher autoimmune incidence than the general population.
  • European and North American cohorts found augmentation patients generally healthier than the general population, with lower standardized mortality ratios.
  • A fibromyalgia association reported in 2001 was criticised as methodologically flawed; the FDA found no support in the literature.
  • A 25,000-woman Canadian mortality study (2006) found breast prostheses do not directly increase mortality.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Fat-graft augmentation

Autologous fat grafting: indications, injection techniques, external tissue expansion, post-mastectomy reconstruction and technical limits.

Fat-graft breast augmentation

Article section

Autologous fat injection for reconstruction, congenital defect correction and aesthetic enhancement — history, evidence and risks.

  • Indications: post-mastectomy reconstruction, trauma and explantation deformity; micromastia, tuberous breast deformity and Poland syndrome; and primary aesthetic augmentation.
  • Developed by Melvin Bircoll; in 1987 Eduardo Krulig injected grafts with a syringe and blunt needle using a disposable fat trap.
  • Up to about 300 ml of body fat can be injected in three equal-volume injections across subpectoral, intrapectoral and submammary spaces.
  • Risks: fat necrosis, metastatic calcification, cysts and palpable lumps.
  • Adding adipose-derived stem cells raised graft success rates in a 2007 40-patient study.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Fat grafting techniques

Article section

Harvesting, centrifugal refinement, blunt-cannula injection in small aliquots, and how much of the graft survives.

  • Only about 25–50% of transferred fat survives at one year, so compensatory over-filling is used.
  • Small-aliquot blunt-cannula injection maximises contact with vascularised tissue and minimises fat necrosis.
  • Contours are sculpted by layering grafts at different depths — from the chest wall to just under the skin.
  • Operating time: about 2 hours for the first 100 cm³, then about 45 minutes per extra 100 cm³.
  • Fat grafted around an implant can hide device edges and wrinkles and soften the capsule.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

External tissue expansion

Article section

Vacuum pre-expansion of the recipient site before fat grafting, with the reported volume gains from two studies.

  • In a 17-woman study, a bra-like vacuum system applied 20 mmHg for 10–12 hours daily over 10 weeks.
  • Average volume gain at week 10 was about 98%, with a stable long-term increase of 55% (range 15–115%).
  • A 2010 study of 25 patients (46 breasts) reported significant volume increases of 60–200% at six months by MRI, with no oil cysts or abnormality.
  • MRI and 3-D volumetric imaging are used to monitor graft viability and volume maintenance.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Post-mastectomy procedures

Article section

Implant and flap reconstruction options, and fat-graft reconstruction as a non-implant alternative.

  • Surgical options include implants, TRAM flap, latissimus myocutaneous flap and DIEP flap.
  • Fat-graft reconstruction begins with 3–5 weeks of external vacuum expansion, then serial grafting sessions over about three months.
  • Some reconstructions begin in the operating room at the mastectomy itself, seeding fat into the recipient site.
  • Reported outcomes: natural form and near-normal sensation, with resumption of normal activities at about 3 days.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Tissue engineering: the breast mound and explantation deformity

Article section

Pre-expanded, fat-seeded breast mounds after mastectomy, and using fat grafts to correct empty implant pockets after explantation.

  • A 2010 series: 33 women (47 breasts) pre-expanded for 10 hours daily over 10–30 days, then grafted with 150–600 ml per session across 2–5 outpatient procedures.
  • Stable reconstructed volumes of 300–600 ml per breast at six months, with benign oil cysts and rare complications (pneumothorax, transient cysts).
  • After implant removal, fat grafts replace about 50% of the removed volume as permanent augmentation.
  • Fat cannot survive in an empty implant pocket — it must be injected into a vascularised tissue matrix.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Fat-graft augmentation outcomes and limitations

Article section

Reported volume gains from fat grafting and why it cannot replace the volumes implants deliver.

  • A 2010 study of 25 patients: mean breast volume increased 1.2× (60–80%, about 250 cm³ per breast) at six months, confirmed by quantitative MRI.
  • Graft volumes of 220–650 cm³ per breast; mean operating time 2 hours; no infection, cyst, seroma, haematoma or necrosis reported.
  • Structural fat grafting gives precise contour control but cannot achieve the large global volume increases implants provide.
  • In one session, even patients with ample donor fat gained about one bra cup size.
  • Radiotherapy of an implant-augmented breast sharply raises complication rates (contracture, infection, extrusion, poor cosmetic outcome).

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Function and safety

Breastfeeding with implants, breast-filler toxicity and platinum toxicity.

Breastfeeding and the prosthetic breast

Article section

Whether implants interfere with breastfeeding, and which surgical choices preserve lactation.

  • Women with implants can breastfeed, but surgery that cuts into the nipple-areola complex can damage ducts or nerves.
  • IMF, transaxillary and transumbilical approaches avoid the nipple-areola complex.
  • Subglandular placement and oversized implants interfere most with lactation; small implants in a submuscular pocket interfere least.
  • Filler leakage into milk is considered a minimal risk: silicone is indigestible and saline digestible.
  • A 1996 study found no causal link between prostheses and impaired breastfeeding function.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Breast-filler toxicity and platinum toxicity

Article section

Theoretical filler transfer to milk, and the platinum catalyst used to make silicone gel — both reviewed as minimal risks.

  • Breast-filler toxicity is described as a minimal risk to a nursing infant because silicone is indigestible and saline digestible.
  • Platinum (Pt 78) is the catalyst that turns liquid silicone oil into gel; trace platinum could theoretically accumulate in bone marrow.
  • The FDA found the platinum in modern implants is not ionised and poses no biological risk, with no reported cases of trace-platinum toxicity.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

The patient

Psychology before surgery, outcomes reported afterwards, women bodybuilders and mental-health findings.

Psychology of breast-augmentation patients

Article section

Mental-health characteristics of women seeking augmentation, and the outcomes they report after surgery.

  • Pre-operative studies report more prior psychotherapy, low self-esteem, depression and body dysmorphia than in the general population.
  • Post-operative surveys report improved physical health, appearance, social life, confidence, self-esteem and sexual functioning.
  • Most women report long-term satisfaction with their implants, even after revision surgery.
  • About 8% of Danish augmentation patients had a pre-operative psychiatric hospitalization history.

Read this section on Wikipedia →

Mental health and mortality findings

Article section

Suicide and mortality findings, and measured self-esteem gains — with the article's conclusion on causation.

  • A 2007 longitudinal study found higher suicide rates among women with implants over time, alongside higher alcohol- and drug-related death risk.
  • The article's conclusion: surgery does not increase suicide risk — it is the psychologically affected woman who is more likely to seek augmentation.
  • A 2007 study reported self-esteem gains of 20.7–24.9 points on the 30-point Rosenberg scale after surgery.
  • Plastic surgeons are advised to assess mental health before operating, to judge whether implants can genuinely help.

Surgical technique

Five types of surgical incision

How the prosthesis reaches the implant pocket — and what each route means for scars, access and breastfeeding.

Five types of surgical incision
IncisionWhat the article says
Inframammary incisionA cut at the inframammary fold (the bottom border of the breast) giving maximal access to the interior of the breast for precise pocket creation and implant placement. Scarring can be noticeable depending on skin type.
Periareolar incisionA short (~5 cm) cut along the lower half of the areola's outer border. The narrow access makes large silicone implants harder to place, tends toward higher capsular contracture rates long term, and risks damaging milk ducts and nerves of the nipple-areola complex, which can impede breastfeeding. It also permits a concurrent breast lift.
Transaxillary incisionA cut in the armpit with a tunnel under the skin to the breast pocket, done bluntly or with an endoscope. It avoids scarring the breast skin; the challenge is judging the ideal implant position for symmetry.
Transumbilical incision (TUBA)An endoscopic approach through the navel, tunneling upward under the abdominal skin to place a saline implant. It avoids scarring the breast skin.
Transabdominal incision (TABA)An endoscopic approach through the navel tunneling up to the breast pocket, performed while the patient simultaneously undergoes an abdominoplasty.

Condensed from the “Types of surgical incision” section. The incision route is chosen with the surgeon according to anatomy, implant type and goals.

Surgical technique

Four implant-pocket placements

Placements described in anatomical relation to the pectoralis major muscle.

Four implant-pocket placements
PlacementWhat the article says
SubglandularThe implant sits between the breast tissue and the pectoralis major muscle (retromammary space), closest to the natural breast plane and usually the most aesthetic — but more prone to visible rippling in women with little soft tissue.
SubfascialThe implant is placed beneath the fascia covering the pectoralis major muscle, to add size and volume for later contouring.
Subpectoral (dual plane)The implant is placed beneath the pectoralis major muscle after partially releasing its lower attachments: the upper half of the implant is covered by muscle, the lower half sits in the subglandular plane. It maximizes upper coverage and lower expansion, at some risk of animation deformity (the implant moving with the muscle).
SubmuscularThe implant is placed entirely beneath the pectoralis major muscle without cutting its lower origin; total coverage can be completed by releasing and reattaching lateral chest-wall muscles (serratus or pectoralis minor).

Condensed from the “Implant-pocket placement” section. Placement affects coverage, rippling risk, recovery and how the implant moves.

Implant types

The four prosthesis types

The four categories of breast prosthesis the article describes, two of which are discontinued.

The four prosthesis types
ProsthesisCategorySummaryDetail
Saline breast prosthesisImplant typeA silicone-elastic shell filled with sterile saline solution in the operating room.First sold commercially by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964. The empty shell is inserted through a short incision, then filled with saline and contoured for symmetry. Results are good to excellent, but rippling and wrinkling of the skin can show, especially in women with little breast tissue; with ample tissue and submuscular placement, results resemble those of silicone-gel implants.
Silicone-gel breast prosthesisImplant typeA shell filled with viscous silicone gel; the technology has passed through five generations of design.Invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used in augmentation in 1962. Generation 1 (1963) was a teardrop silicone-rubber sack with a Dacron fastener patch. Generation 2 (1970s) used thin shells and low-cohesion gel — fragile, with higher rupture, leakage and capsular contracture rates that prompted class-action lawsuits; polyurethane-coated variants reduced contracture but were dropped in the U.S. over carcinogenic TDA by-products (they remain in use in Europe and South America); double-lumen designs combined gel and saline with post-operative volume adjustability. Generations 3 and 4 (1980s) added elastomer coatings to reduce gel bleed, with shaped, tapered and round textured or smooth models. Generation 5 (1990s) uses semi-solid cohesive gel that resists leakage and migration, with studies reporting lower capsular contracture and rupture rates than earlier generations.
Alternative-composition breast prosthesisImplant type (discontinued)Fillers such as soy oil, polypropylene string, ox cartilage, Terylene wool, ground rubber, silastic or Teflon-silicone — now discontinued.The article lists these fillers as substances harmful to the body and no longer in use.
Structured breast prosthesisImplant type (discontinued)Nested silicone-rubber shells with saline between them, approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; now discontinued.Three nested shells support the upper half of the breast and the two spaces between them are filled with saline, combining saline and silicone technologies. The folded empty device is inserted, then filled with saline and the incision sutured.

Condensed from the “Breast-augmentation prostheses” section. Implant availability differs by country and regulator.

Extracted data

Key facts from the article

The statements below condense what the Wikipedia article says about breast augmentation. The right-hand column links to the source article.

Key facts from the article
TopicWhat the article saysSource
DefinitionBreast augmentation (also breast enlargement) is a plastic surgery procedure placing a breast implant or fat graft on the thorax to increase breast size, correct congenital defects and restore anatomic proportion.Breast augmentation
Three purposesProsthetic breasts are placed for three therapeutic reasons: primary reconstruction after cancer, trauma or developmental defect; revision of a previous mammoplasty; and primary aesthetic augmentation.Breast augmentation
Fat-graft gainA fat-graft augmentation yields a modest size increase — usually about one bra cup size — because the body resorbs much of the injected fat.Breast augmentation
Saline historyThe first commercial saline-filled breast prosthesis was presented by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964.Breast augmentation
Silicone historyThe silicone-gel implant was invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used for augmentation in 1962; its technology spans five generations.Breast augmentation
Structured implantsStructured (nested-shell) breast prostheses were approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; both structured and alternative-composition prostheses are now discontinued.Breast augmentation
IncisionsFive surgical incision routes are used: inframammary, periareolar, transaxillary, transumbilical (TUBA) and transabdominal (TABA).Breast augmentation
PlacementsFour implant-pocket placements are described: subglandular, subfascial, subpectoral (dual plane) and submuscular.Breast augmentation
RecoveryScars heal at about 6 weeks, most patients resume normal activities at about 1 week, and strenuous exercise is avoided for about 6 weeks; submuscular placement means a longer, more painful recovery.Breast augmentation
Complication rateComplications from implant surgery and tissue expanders occur in approximately 6–7% of breast-augmentation patients.Breast augmentation
Explantation at 10 yearsAbout 20% of women with aesthetic implants and 50% of reconstruction patients required explantation of a failed prosthesis at the 10-year mark.Breast augmentation
BIA-ALCL recallIn 2019 the FDA recalled all Allergan Biocell textured breast prostheses after a causal link was identified with BIA-ALCL, an immune-system cancer.Breast augmentation
Rupture detectionManual examination detects only about 30% of implant ruptures, while MRI detects about 86%; the FDA recommends screening MRI at 3 years post-surgery and every 2 years thereafter for suspected rupture.Breast augmentation
Saline rupture ratesReported saline rupture-and-deflation rates are 3–5% at 3 years and 7–10% at 10 years; overfilling implants by about 10–13% reduced the 8-year deflation rate to 1.83%.Breast augmentation
Revision ratesRevision (re-operation) rates were reported as 20% at 3 years and 3.0% at 7 years in the article's cited Tebbetts data.Breast augmentation
Systemic diseaseReviews and longitudinal studies since the 1990s consistently report no causal relation between silicone-gel implants and systemic or autoimmune disease.Breast augmentation
Fat survivalOnly about 25–50% of a fat graft survives at one year, so grafts are deliberately over-filled; retained contours typically last 18–24 months.Breast augmentation
Fat-graft volume gainA 2010 clinical-radiological study reported a mean breast-volume increase of 1.2× (60–80%, about 250 cm³ per breast) at 6 months after fat grafting, confirmed by quantitative MRI.Breast augmentation
External expansionExternal vacuum pre-expansion (20 mmHg, 10–12 hours daily for 10 weeks) produced an average 98% volume gain at week 10, settling to a stable 55% long-term increase (range 15–115%).Breast augmentation
BreastfeedingSmall implants in a submuscular pocket interfere least with breastfeeding; subglandular placement and oversized implants interfere most, and IMF/TABA/TUBA approaches avoid the nipple-areola complex.Breast augmentation
Self-esteemA 2007 study reported post-operative self-esteem increases of 20.7–24.9 points on the 30-point Rosenberg scale, alongside reports of improved confidence and sexual functioning.Breast augmentation
Mental-health cautionThe article notes higher pre-operative rates of depression, low self-esteem and body dysmorphia among augmentation seekers, and concludes that underlying psychological factors — not the surgery itself — explain the suicide-risk correlation reported in longitudinal studies.Breast augmentation
RadiotherapyRadiotherapy of an implant-augmented breast much increases complication rates — capsular contracture, infection, extrusion and poor cosmetic outcome — which can preclude conservative breast surgery.Breast augmentation

Statements are paraphrased from the Wikipedia article. Wikipedia is open content that anyone can edit; verify against the linked article revision before relying on any point.
